docs.title: Irrigated Cropland Mapping with Geospatial Foundation Models
docs.text:
Evaluating geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs) for irrigated cropland mapping in North Africa and their transferability to data-scarce regions

Irrigated agriculture covers about a fifth of the world's cropland but produces around 40% of its food and accounts for most freshwater withdrawals. Knowing where and how much land is irrigated is therefore essential for water management and food security, especially in water-stressed regions such as North Africa. Yet most countries lack accurate, regularly updated irrigation maps, and existing global products are coarse or static. Geospatial foundation models, large models pretrained on vast archives of satellite imagery, promise accurate maps from few labels and better transfer to new regions. This research evaluates that promise for irrigated cropland mapping, using Morocco as a case study. It asks how accurately these models separate irrigated from rainfed cropland compared with conventional satellite-based methods, how much adapting them to the task helps, how consistent their maps are from year to year, and how well a model trained in Morocco transfers to a region with little ground truth.

docs.title: D1. Spatial folds instead of a 70/30 split
docs.text:
• Proposal (§4.1): stratified 70 / 30 split, validation subset from the training data. (§4.2.4 already asks for spatial cross-validation.)
  • Now: parcels grouped into 20 km blocks, blocks into 5 folds with equal class balance; every parcel tested once by a model that never saw its block.
  • Why: with a random split, 79% of test parcels lie within 250 m of a training parcel (about 2% with 20 km blocks). Random splits overstate accuracy for mapping new areas (Roberts et al. 2017; Ploton et al. 2020).
  • Where: dataset §5, protocol §2.

docs.title: D2. Two agricultural years (per-parcel season)
docs.text:
• Proposal (§4.1): the 2024 annual image stack.
  • Now: each parcel gets the 12 months (1 Sep – 31 Aug) of the season in which it was surveyed: 2023/24 or 2024/25. Both seasons in one dataset, months aligned (month 1 = September).
  • Why: the survey ran Dec 2023 – Jan 2025; using only 2024 would mix seasons, and dropping 2024/25 would lose 42% of the rainfed parcels. The agricultural year covers the winter rainfed cycle and the summer, when only irrigated fields stay green.
  • Consequence: region and year are partly confounded (Gharb and Tadla only 2023/24, Souss only 2024/25).
  • Where: dataset §6.2.

docs.title: D3. Validation: PASTIS rotation instead of nested CV
docs.text:
• Before (E01): nested spatial CV, settings by inner CV on the 4 training folds, refit on 4.
  • Now: per round 3 folds train, the next fold chooses the settings (or stops training), 1 fold tests, as in PASTIS (Garnot & Landrieu 2021).
  • Why: one design for classical classifiers and neural networks (L-TAE, fine-tuning), which need a separate validation fold for early stopping. It is the standard design of the PASTIS crop-mapping benchmark.
  • Where: protocol §2; E01 is kept as the sensitivity check.

docs.title: D4. One shared tile store for every input
docs.text:
• Proposal: annual Sentinel-1/2 composites via STAC and xarray.
  • Now: Google Earth Engine builds non-overlapping 128 × 128 px tiles (1.28 km) with 12 monthly composites × 19 bands; the baseline features and the foundation-model chips are all cut from these tiles.
  • Why: STAC processing was too slow for the full set; with one store every input sees identical pixels, compositing and masks, and chips no longer overlap across folds.
  • Where: dataset §6–7.

docs.title: D5. Frozen encoder + classical classifiers
docs.text:
• Proposal (§4.2.1): frozen encoder, train a decoder and classification head.
  • Now: the task is per parcel, so the frozen encoder gives one embedding per parcel and the "head" is a classifier (linear probe and three others). Fine-tuning (LoRA, RQ2) follows as planned.
  • Why: tests what the pretrained representation already contains, at equal cost for every model; the linear probe is the standard test of frozen features.

docs.title: D6. Four classifiers instead of one Random Forest
docs.text:
• Proposal: Random Forest baseline.
  • Now: logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting and SVM on every input (RF stays the headline).
  • Why: a classifier that suits hand-built features (RF) may not suit dense embeddings (E01: RF is the weakest classifier on embeddings). Reporting all four keeps the comparison from depending on one choice.

docs.title: D7. Macro-F1 as the headline metric
docs.text:
• Proposal (§4.2.4): OA, precision, recall, F1; best model by mean F1 over the five folds, SD as consistency.
  • Now: macro-F1 of all out-of-fold predictions with a 95% block-bootstrap CI as headline; per-fold mean ± SD is reported too, as the proposal asked.
  • Why: with 86% irrigated parcels, overall accuracy and irrigated F1 are high for any model; macro-F1 weights the rainfed class equally. Paired bootstrap differences say whether a gap is real.

docs.title: D8. Two temporal aggregation pipelines
docs.text:
• Proposal: not specified.
  • Now: PCA pipeline (concat 12 months → PCA 128) in E01 / E02; L-TAE pipeline in E03.
  • Why: PANGAEA (Marsocci et al. 2024) found L-TAE better than linear mapping for single-date encoders; testing both shows whether the conclusion depends on how the months are combined.
  • Where: protocol §5.

docs.title: D9. Cloud Score+ instead of QA60
docs.text:
• Now: Sentinel-2 pixels kept when Cloud Score+ cs_cdf ≥ 0.60; scenes with up to 60% cloud admitted.
  • Why: the QA60 band misses thin cloud and shadow; Cloud Score+ is the recommended mask in Earth Engine (Pasquarella et al. 2023).

docs.title: D10. Transfer region under review
docs.text:
• Proposal (§3.2): zero-shot transfer to Tunisia, validated on 54 GMIA-NEXT points (44 irrigated, 10 rainfed).
  • Now: Morocco first. As an alternative, US state datasets with both irrigated and dryland fields (eastern Washington WSDA, Utah WRLU 2017–2025) would allow a spatial and a multi-year test with the same pipeline.
  • Why: 10 rainfed points are too few to measure a rainfed F1; the US data needs a check of its labels (see the progress log, 4–5 Nov 2026).
  • Decision due: after RQ1 and RQ2.

docs.title: D11. Two kinds of head: parcel benchmark and mapping model
docs.text:
• Proposal (§4.2.1, §4.3): frozen encoder with a decoder / head; annual irrigated maps 2021–2025 for Morocco.
  • Problem: the RQ1 pipeline pools the embeddings over the parcel polygon. Annual maps of Morocco (or of a transfer region) have no polygons, and the GeoFM patches (80 m Clay, 160 m the others) are too coarse for parcels of 0.83 ha (median, about 90 m across).
  • Now:
  • RQ1 benchmark (unchanged): frozen encoder → parcel embedding → LogReg (linear probe), RF, HGB, SVM; plus L-TAE + MLP head (E03). Classical heads on frozen embeddings are common practice (Presto; WorldCereal; AlphaEarth irrigated mapping, Yang et al. 2026) and the head matters little in recent comparisons (Mughees et al. 2026).
  • Mapping models (RQ2–RQ4): frozen GeoFM + UPerNet segmentation head trained on the label pixels of the tiles (as in PANGAEA and Prithvi-EO-2.0), then LoRA with the same head (RQ2). Classical baseline: RF on the S1/S2 features of each pixel.
  • Neural baselines from scratch: TempCNN (per-pixel time series; Pelletier et al. 2019) and U-TAE (tiles; Garnot & Landrieu 2021). Both produce 10 m maps. PSE-TAE needs parcel polygons and stays a parcel-level extra (E04).
  • Same scoring: pixel predictions are aggregated per parcel (mean probability) and scored with the same folds, parcels and bootstrap as RQ1, so every number stays comparable.
  • Why: the research must end in wall-to-wall annual maps; a 1D-CNN beat RF for irrigated mapping (Bazzi et al. 2019) and TempCNN-type models transferred better across regions than GeoFM embeddings (Tong & Wang 2025), so a neural baseline is needed next to the classical one.
  • Where: literature notes.

docs.title: D12. AgriFM with its pretrained 4-px patch embedding
docs.text:
• Before: 02d_embed_agrifm.py built the Sentinel-2 encoder with the patch size of the repository's fine-tuning configuration (configs/cropland_mapping.py: 4 time steps × 2 × 2 px, output stride 16 px) and loaded AgriFM.pth through mmengine. No weight was loaded: the checkpoint names carry the prefix encoder., and the pretrained patch embedding (S2_patch_emd, kernel 128 × 10 × 4 × 4 × 4) does not fit a 2 × 2 px patch. mmengine only warns about mismatched names and still reports success, so all AgriFM embeddings produced up to 6 Nov 2026 (local and on the cluster, including E01) came from a randomly initialised encoder.
  • Now: patch size 4 × 4 × 4 (the size of the pretrained patch embedding), output stride 32 px (320 m; 2 × 2 cells per 64-px chip). The weights are mapped by name in the script and every encoder tensor must load; otherwise the script stops. On the cluster 349 of 349 encoder tensors load.
  • Why: the frozen-encoder comparison (D5) must use each encoder as pretrained. In the fine-tuning set-up of the repository the 2 × 2 px patch embedding is trained anew; with a frozen encoder it would stay random. The alternative, resizing the 4 × 4 px kernel to 2 × 2 px, keeps a finer grid but replaces the pretrained first layer by an approximation.
  • Consequence: AgriFM has the coarsest grid of the four models (320 m against 80–160 m), which matters for small parcels; the patch-share weighting is unchanged. Earlier AgriFM results are void and are re-run.
  • Where: models_run/02d_embed_agrifm.py, Foundation models · inputs.

docs.title: Foundation models
docs.text: This page is the single reference for the four geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs) evaluated in this study. It summarises their design and pretraining, specifies how each model is applied to the Moroccan parcels, and lists the primary sources. Other pages refer to this page rather than repeating its content.

docs.title: Selection
docs.text: The four models were selected according to three criteria: (i) pretrained weights are openly available and can be fine-tuned; (ii) the models accept multi-temporal Sentinel-1 and/or Sentinel-2 input; and (iii) together they represent the principal GeoFM families, namely masked-autoencoder Vision Transformers (Prithvi-EO-2.0, Clay), a multimodal generative model (TerraMind) and an agriculture-specific spatio-temporal model (AgriFM).

docs.title: Configuration in this study
docs.text:
All encoders are used frozen, i.e. as fixed feature extractors without gradient updates. Each model receives a 64 × 64 px chip (640 m) centred on the parcel, with the bands and normalisation statistics of its own pretraining. The parcel embedding is the mean of the patch tokens covering the parcel, weighted by the fraction of each patch inside the parcel (Models pipeline §5). The Sentinel-1/2 feature baseline is listed for comparison.

Input Chips Bands Patch Temporal handling Output per parcel Script S1/S2 baseline parcel features (inner pixels) 12 S2 bands, NDVI, NDWI, EVI, S1 VV and VH (one orbit) parcel median 12 months concatenated 204 features 03 Clay v1.5 p8 10 S2 bands 8 px (80 m) one month per forward pass 12 × 1024 02a Prithvi-EO-2.0 p16 6 S2 bands (HLS set) 16 px (160 m) four months per pass, three passes 12 × 1024 02b TerraMind p16 12 S2 bands, S1 VV and VH 16 px (160 m) one month per forward pass 12 × 768 02c AgriFM p16 10 S2 bands 4 px pretrained patch embedding; output stride 32 px (320 m) full 12-month stack in one pass 1 × 1024 02d

TerraMind is the only model that receives Sentinel-1, because it is the only one pretrained on SAR data. Two sensitivity runs isolate the contribution of radar: an optical-only baseline (S1S2_VARIABLES = "s2" in script 03) and TerraMind with optical input only (MODALITIES = ["S2L2A"] in script 02c).

docs.title: Clay v1.5
docs.text: Clay encodes each band together with its central wavelength, which allows a single model to process imagery from different sensors. Ten Sentinel-2 bands (B2–B8A, B11, B12) are standardised with the statistics of Clay's metadata.yaml. Additional inputs are the pixel size (10 m), the acquisition date (week of year, sine/cosine encoded; monthly composites are dated mid-month) and the location (latitude and longitude, sine/cosine encoded). The model processes one date per forward pass, so the twelve months are embedded independently. With 8 px patches, a chip yields an 8 × 8 token grid.

docs.title: Prithvi-EO-2.0-300M-TL
docs.text: Prithvi-EO-2.0 is pretrained on HLS time series and encodes acquisition date and location explicitly. The six HLS bands (Blue, Green, Red, Narrow NIR, SWIR 1, SWIR 2; Sentinel-2 B2, B3, B4, B8A, B11, B12) are standardised with the model's pretraining statistics. Following the pretraining configuration, four frames are processed per pass (September–December, January–April, May–August); each frame retains its own tokens, giving one vector per month. The model is loaded through TerraTorch (prithvi_eo_v2_300_tl). Limitation: pretraining used 30 m HLS data, whereas 10 m Sentinel-2 is used here; the resulting 160 m patch is closer to typical parcel size than the 480 m patch at native resolution.

docs.title: TerraMind-1.0-base
docs.text: TerraMind is trained to generate any of nine modalities from any other and therefore learns a joint representation of optical, radar and auxiliary data. Two modalities are supplied: S2L2A (B1–B12) and S1GRD (VV, VH in dB), each standardised with TerraMind's pretraining statistics. The tokens of the two modalities are averaged (merge_method = "mean"). One date is processed per pass, and 16 px patches give a 4 × 4 token grid.

docs.title: AgriFM
docs.text: AgriFM is designed for crop mapping and models the temporal dimension within the network. The full 12-month stack of ten Sentinel-2 bands is processed in a single pass, normalised with the repository's cropland_mapping.py configuration. Input tokens span four time steps and 2 × 2 px; the final feature map has a stride of 16 px. Because time is compressed inside the network, the output is one vector per parcel and season. Only the encoder is used, through the mmengine registries of the cloned repository. Open point: the configuration's normalisation mean (e.g. ~4,180 for the blue band) is well above typical Sentinel-2 L2A reflectance values (~1,100); the expected pixel scale is being verified before AgriFM results are reported as final.

docs.title: Why irrigated cropland matters
docs.text:
Irrigated agriculture covers only about 20% of the world's cultivated land, yet it produces around 40% of global food and accounts for about 70% of all freshwater withdrawals (Wu et al., 2023). With population growth, climate change and increasing water scarcity, reliable information on where irrigation takes place, and how it changes from year to year, is essential for water management, agricultural planning and the Sustainable Development Goals on food (SDG 2) and water (SDG 6).

Morocco is a demanding and relevant case. Agriculture provides about 14% of its GDP, 39% of national employment and 74% of rural employment, and the country has developed more than two million hectares of irrigated land across seven large schemes. At the same time it is among the most water-stressed countries in the world: agriculture uses over 80% of the available water, while rainfall has fallen by about 30% over three decades. National programmes (the Green Morocco Plan 2008–2020 and the Green Generation strategy 2020–2030) expanded drip irrigation from 160,000 ha in 2008 to 585,000 ha in 2019 (Guemouria et al., 2023). Tracking whether this expansion meets its goals, and where water use is most intensive, requires precise and up-to-date irrigated cropland maps.

Much of the rest of North Africa lacks the dense, field-verified irrigation data that exists for Morocco. Methods that can be trained where labels are rich and transferred to agro-climatically similar, data-scarce regions would be a significant step for agricultural monitoring across the region.

docs.title: State of the art
docs.text:
Approach Examples Limitation Global irrigation products GMIA (Siebert et al., 2005; ~9 km), GIAM (Thenkabail et al., 2009) far too coarse for fields of a few hectares 30 m global maps LGRIP30 (Teluguntla et al., 2023; 86.5% overall accuracy), GMIE (Wu et al., 2023) static snapshots or decade-maximum extents, no annual series; locally calibrated thresholds Machine learning on Sentinel-1/2 time series current state of the art for field-scale irrigation mapping depends on hand-built spectral and temporal features; degrades when applied to new regions; hard to combine sensors (Yang et al., 2026)

Geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs) offer a different route. They are large neural networks pretrained with self-supervised learning on vast unlabelled satellite archives. They learn rich spatio-temporal representations directly from the imagery, without hand-built features, can be adapted to a task with few labels, and may transfer across regions and sensors (Tseng et al., 2023; Szwarcman et al., 2024). Adaptation ranges from a frozen encoder with a light classification head, through parameter-efficient fine-tuning such as LoRA, to full fine-tuning.

docs.title: Research gap
docs.text:
1. No annual irrigated cropland maps exist for Morocco or other North African countries. Global products give static extents, not the year-by-year maps needed to monitor irrigation expansion and evaluate policy. This needs a model that is accurate and consistent from one year to the next.
  2. No geospatial foundation model has been evaluated for irrigated cropland mapping, and none in Africa's diverse agro-hydrological landscapes, from semi-arid to sub-humid climates and from flood to drip and pivot irrigation.
  3. It is unknown which foundation model suits the task best, how much fine-tuning adds to a frozen encoder, and whether a model trained in one region still works in a data-scarce region nearby.

docs.title: Objectives and research questions
docs.text:
Main objective: to compare the performance and transferability of geospatial foundation models for irrigated cropland mapping.

Objective Research question 1 · Compare models and adaptation strategies in Morocco RQ1 What classification accuracy does each foundation model achieve for irrigated cropland mapping across Morocco's agricultural regions, and how does it compare with a conventional Sentinel-based classifier? RQ2 To what extent does parameter-efficient fine-tuning improve on a frozen encoder? 2 · Evaluate temporal and spatial transferability of the best model RQ3 How temporally consistent is the best model across years, and does the annual map series for Morocco (2021–2025) reflect the irrigation trends in national statistics? RQ4 When the Morocco-trained model is applied without retraining to another region, how much does accuracy degrade, and do its annual maps stay consistent? 3 · Optional extension: multi-model fusion RQ5 Does fusing the embeddings of several foundation models improve on the best single model?

docs.title: Study area and data
docs.text:
Morocco. Five major agricultural regions that together span the country's diversity (Ouassanouan et al., 2026):

Region Climate Irrigation and crops El Gharb humid surface-water irrigation; rice, vegetables Tadla semi-arid to sub-humid large-scale irrigation; sugar beet, cereals Doukkala Mediterranean mixed irrigated and rainfed systems El Haouz semi-arid groundwater irrigation; olives, citrus Souss arid advanced drip systems; high-value export crops

Transfer region. The proposal applies the best Morocco-trained model, without retraining, to Tunisia, which shares Morocco's Mediterranean to semi-arid climate, crops and irrigation types but lacks parcel-level ground truth; it would be validated with the GMIA-NEXT reference points (Kebede et al., 2026). The choice of transfer region is under review (decision D10).

Data Use Field survey, Ouassanouan et al. (2026): 8,826 georeferenced parcels with crop type, irrigation status and irrigation system (8,781 after cleaning: 7,585 irrigated, 1,196 rainfed) training and validation in Morocco Sentinel-2 multispectral (10 m) and Sentinel-1 SAR (VV, VH) time series model input GMIE, LGRIP30, FAO WaPOR, FAO AQUASTAT comparison of the maps with existing products and national statistics

docs.title: Models compared
docs.text: Four openly available GeoFMs are evaluated: Prithvi-EO-2.0 (NASA, IBM), Clay v1.5 (Clay Foundation), TerraMind (IBM, ESA) and AgriFM (Li et al., 2025). They accept multi-temporal Sentinel-1/2 input and together represent the principal GeoFM families: masked-autoencoder Vision Transformers, a multimodal generative model and an agriculture-specific spatio-temporal model. Architecture, pretraining, configuration and sources are given in Foundation models.

docs.title: Expected outcomes
docs.text:
1. A comprehensive evaluation of four geospatial foundation models for irrigated cropland mapping in North Africa, against a strong Sentinel-based baseline under spatial validation.
  2. A comparison of frozen-encoder and parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategies for this task.
  3. Annual irrigated cropland maps for Morocco at 10 m resolution for 2021–2025, checked against national statistics.
  4. An assessment of the temporal consistency of foundation-model predictions across years.
  5. An assessment of how far the best model transfers to a data-scarce region.
  6. A reusable, ML-ready dataset of irrigated and rainfed parcels with spatial folds.

docs.title: 2026-11-04 (future phase: US data for spatial and temporal transfer — decision deferred)
docs.text: Discussed after reading IrrMap (Mandal et al. 2025, arXiv:2505.08273). Decision: complete Morocco first; come back to this later. - IrrMap itself is not usable as the study area. It labels irrigation method (flood / sprinkler / drip, all else "other"); there is no rainfed class, so irrigated vs rainfed cannot be studied with it. Its labels come from state agency maps (not field survey); inputs are single-season 224 px patches; validation is a random 80/20 split per state, with no validation split and no spatial test; only a U-Net (ResNet-34) is benchmarked, no GeoFMs. -> Keep Morocco as the AOI (field-surveyed labels, data-scarce region, 12-month time series, spatial folds). Cite IrrMap as related work and as a model for the dataset paper (Part 1). - Idea for a second phase: use the original field boundaries and labels behind IrrMap (state datasets), build chips from scratch with the same pipeline (labels -> 20 km block folds -> tile store -> chips -> embeddings -> same classifiers and validation), to test spatial and temporal transferability. - Why it is valuable: state data often covers many years over the same fields -> clean temporal transfer (train earlier years, test later years), which Morocco cannot offer (year and region overlap); a second continent tests whether GeoFMs transfer better than S1/S2 features (Morocco <-> US). - Conditions: (1) the source data must contain non-irrigated / dryland parcels (deal-breaker; e.g. Washington agricultural land-use data includes dryland wheat — to be checked state by state); (2) small scope: 1-2 states, 3-4 years, ~10-20k parcels; (3) only after Morocco is finished. - Pipeline changes needed: new label reader in ml_dataset_prep/01_prepare_labels.py; support other UTM zones in 03_build_tiles.py (now fixed to UTM 29N; western US spans zones 10-13); US season window via START_MONTH; optional fold by year in 02; a new transfer evaluation (train region/year A, test B). models_run/ unchanged. - Risks: administrative (noisier) labels; different crop systems (Morocco <-> US transfer may be poor for all models); ~4-8 extra weeks. - First step when resuming: one-day check of which state sources IrrMap used, whether they include dryland / non-irrigated fields, which years, and whether field boundaries are downloadable. - Fallback if the check fails: keep as future work; use GMIA-NEXT ground-truth points (tools/a1) or Tunisia as the external test.

Same scheme as PASTIS (Garnot & Landrieu 2021) and 03b_train_psetae.py, so classifiers and the neural-network baseline are trained, tuned and tested identically. docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The dataset is complete: 8,781 field-surveyed parcels with Sentinel-1/2 time series of their agricultural year, five spatial folds and a shared tile store. Embeddings of all four foundation models are computed. The first RQ1 experiment shows that no frozen foundation model beats a well-designed Sentinel-1/2 baseline on average (macro-F1 0.910 for the best pair vs 0.906), while Clay and Prithvi hold up better in the hardest region. The main RQ1 run with the final validation design is ready, and a second way of combining the months (L-TAE) is planned. The experiment setup, documentation and website are in place, so every result can be rerun and traced.

docs.title: E01 · Frozen GeoFMs + PCA vs the S1/S2 baseline (nested spatial CV)
docs.text:
Do frozen foundation-model embeddings separate irrigated from rainfed parcels better than Sentinel-1/2 features, with the same parcels, folds and classifiers?

  • Result: best Clay v1.5 + SVM 0.910; best baseline SVM 0.906; 0 of 16 input-classifier pairs better, 2 worse than the baseline (Holm).
  • Answer: No frozen GeoFM beats the S1/S2 baseline (best Clay + SVM 0.910 vs 0.906, difference within the noise); Clay and Prithvi hold up better in the hardest fold.
  • Full report: E01 report

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This page specifies the software environment, the required input data and model weights, the execution order of the scripts and the structure of the repository.

docs.title: 1. Environment
docs.text:
# creates "condaml" (or: conda env update -n condaml -f environment.yml)
conda env create -f environment.yml                 
conda activate condaml

# Clay (--no-deps: avoids an einops conflict with TerraTorch)
pip install --no-deps git+https://github.com/Clay-foundation/model.git  

# AgriFM
pip install mmengine

A GPU (CUDA or Apple Silicon) is recommended for the embedding scripts. Everything else runs on a CPU.

docs.title: 2. Earth Engine
docs.text: Only ml_dataset_prep/03_build_tiles.py uses Earth Engine. Put the service-account key in secrets/ (path set at the top of the script), or run earthengine authenticate once.

docs.title: 3. Input data
docs.text:
File Source Where Field survey (parcels with land use and irrigation method) Ouassanouan et al. (2026), Scientific Data data/field_survey/lulc_fielddata.shp Morocco boundary GADM 4.1 data/admin/gadm41_MAR_0.json

The Sentinel-1/2 imagery is not downloaded by hand. 03_build_tiles.py fetches it from Earth Engine.

docs.title: 4. Model weights
docs.text:
All weights are stored in checkpoints/<model>/ (excluded from version control) and are downloaded automatically on the first run of each embedding script; later runs reuse them. Folders and sources per model: Foundation models · Weights.

Only the Clay code needs installing by hand (pip install --no-deps git+https://github.com/Clay-foundation/model.git, see Environment above); TerraTorch (Prithvi, TerraMind) and mmengine (AgriFM) come with environment.yml.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
Run every script from the project folder. Each script has its settings at the top. A description at the top of each script explains what it does and what it writes.

# Phase 1 · dataset
python ml_dataset_prep/01_prepare_labels.py
python ml_dataset_prep/02_make_spatial_folds.py
python ml_dataset_prep/03_build_tiles.py       
python ml_dataset_prep/04_make_views.py

# Phase 2 · model evaluation
python models_run/01_inspect_dataset.py          # check the data before training
python models_run/02a_embed_clay.py              # 02a–02d: GPU recommended, resumable
python models_run/02b_embed_prithvi.py
python models_run/02c_embed_terramind.py
python models_run/02d_embed_agrifm.py

# Experiments · training, comparison and report from one config file
python experiments/run_experiment.py             # set EXPERIMENT at the top, e.g. "E02_frozen_pca_pastis"

For a quick check before a full run, set N_TEST_TILES = 20 in 03_build_tiles.py and QUICK_TEST: true in the experiment's config.yaml. How experiments work, and how to add one: Experiments.

docs.text:
Ouassanouan, Y., Elfarkh, J., Grich, S., Liblab, A., & Chehbouni, A. (2026). Crop and irrigation types ground-truth dataset for Moroccan agricultural regions. Scientific Data, 13, 746. doi:10.1038/s41597-026-06993-y

About 10,000 geolocated agricultural parcels were collected across the five major agricultural regions of Morocco (El Gharb, Tadla, Doukkala, El Haouz and Souss) between December 2023 and January 2025, with the GIS mobile application QField. docs.title: How an experiment runs
docs.text:
flowchart LR CFG["<b>config.yaml</b><br/>inputs · steps · settings"] --> RUN["<b>run_experiment.py</b>"] RUN --> S1["<b>train_evaluate</b><br/>models_run/03 · once per input"] RUN --> S2["<b>ltae</b><br/>models_run/03c · once per input"] S1 --> R["results/<run>/<br/>out-of-fold predictions"] S2 --> R R --> C["<b>compare</b><br/>models_run/04<br/>same parcels · paired bootstrap"] C --> REP["<b>report</b><br/>make_report.py"] REP --> MD["docs/experiments/<name>/report.md<br/>experiment list · results page<br/>site menu"] EMB[("outputs/study/02_embeddings<br/>shared by all experiments")] -.-> S1 EMB -.-> S2
  • The scripts in models_run/ are not edited for an experiment. Each has its settings at the top; in experiment mode the values in config.yaml replace them (same names). A misspelt setting stops the run with an error, so a config can never be silently ignored.
  • Embeddings are shared. They depend only on the dataset and the model, so models_run/02a–02d are run once and every experiment reads outputs/study/02_embeddings/.
  • Runs that are finished are skipped, so an interrupted experiment continues where it stopped. RERUN = True (or deleting results/) repeats it.
  • results/run_info.json keeps the config, the git commit and the dates of every run, so a result can always be traced back to the code that produced it.

docs.title: Two pipelines for the monthly embeddings
docs.text:
The foundation models produce one embedding per month (Clay, Prithvi-EO-2.0, TerraMind) or one per agricultural year (AgriFM). The two pipelines differ only in how the monthly embeddings are aggregated; all preceding and subsequent steps are shared.

flowchart LR E["Monthly embeddings<br/>12 × D per parcel"] --> P1["<b>PCA pipeline</b> (E01, E02)<br/>concat 12 months → standardise → PCA 128"] E --> P2["<b>L-TAE pipeline</b> (E03)<br/>attention over the 12 months (trained)"] P1 --> K["LogReg · RF · HGB · SVM"] P2 --> H["MLP head"] K --> O["out-of-fold predictions<br/>same format"] H --> O O --> CMP["04_compare_models<br/>same parcels, same bootstrap draws"]

Because both pipelines write the same oof_predictions.csv, the comparison and the report need no change. E03 also lists the E02 runs under compare: EXTRA_RUNS, so PCA and L-TAE are compared on the same parcels and the same bootstrap draws. Details: evaluation protocol §5.

docs.title: Start a new experiment
docs.text:
1. Copy experiments/_template/config.yaml to experiments/E<NN>_<short_name>/config.yaml (next free number; the name says what varies) and experiments/_template/README.md to docs/experiments/E<NN>_<short_name>/index.md.
  2. Edit config.yaml: title, short title (menu), question, changes_from, inputs, steps and only the settings that differ from the script defaults.
  3. Write the setup page index.md: question, why, what changes (a small table against the experiment it builds on).
  4. Set EXPERIMENT = "E<NN>_<short_name>" in run_experiment.py and run it. Use QUICK_TEST: true first to check that everything runs, then set it back to false and delete results/. The report page and the menu entry are created automatically.
  5. When it has finished: write the Answer, Key findings, Interpretation, Caveats and Next steps in report.md (the tables and figures are already there), set status: done and a one-line answer: in the config, run make_report.py once more, and add an entry to the progress log.

A new pipeline variant (another model or aggregation) gets its own script in models_run/ with settings at the top, the experiment-mode block, and the output format of 03_train_evaluate.py; then add it to SCRIPTS in run_experiment.py.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Do frozen foundation-model embeddings separate irrigated from rainfed parcels better than Sentinel-1/2 features, with the same parcels, folds and classifiers?

docs.title: Why
docs.text: First complete run on the shared 128 px tile store with patch-aligned chips: every input sees the same pixels, the same monthly composites and the same parcels, so any difference comes from the representation.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text: Inputs S1/S2 baseline (204 parcel features) · Clay v1.5 (chips p8) · Prithvi-EO-2.0 · TerraMind · AgriFM (chips p16) Encoders frozen; one embedding per parcel per month (AgriFM: per year), patch-share-weighted mean over the parcel Temporal aggregation concat 12 months → standardise → PCA 128 (fitted on the training folds only) Classifiers LogReg (linear probe), RF, HGB, SVM; grids in the protocol Validation nested spatial CV: 5 outer folds (20 km blocks); inner spatial CV on the 4 training folds chooses the hyperparameters; refit on 4 folds

docs.title: How to run again
docs.text:
# experiments/run_experiment.py:  EXPERIMENT = "E01_frozen_pca_nested",  RERUN = True
python experiments/run_experiment.py
About 2 h per foundation-model input and 30 min for the baseline on the MacBook (CPU).

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: No foundation model beats the S1/S2 baseline: the best input-classifier pair is Clay + SVM (macro-F1 0.910) against 0.906 for the baseline with the same SVM, a difference well inside the noise. With a linear probe, Clay and TerraMind equal the baseline; with a random forest every GeoFM is lower, and AgriFM is clearly worse. The GeoFMs do better than the baseline in the hardest test fold. Full report: REPORT.md.

docs.title: E01 · Frozen GeoFMs + PCA vs the S1/S2 baseline (nested spatial CV) — report
docs.text: Answer. No frozen foundation model classifies irrigated vs rainfed parcels better than the Sentinel-1/2 baseline. The best pair, Clay + SVM (macro-F1 0.910), is level with the baseline + SVM (0.906; Δ +0.003, 95% CI −0.022 to +0.030). The embeddings carry about the same information as well-designed monthly S1/S2 features, and they hold up better in the hardest region.

docs.title: Key findings
docs.text:
• No input differs from the baseline after correcting for multiple tests for Clay, Prithvi and TerraMind, whatever the classifier. The four best results lie within 0.005 of each other (0.905–0.910, all with the SVM).
  • Linear probe: TerraMind 0.896, Clay 0.887 and the baseline 0.887 are level. The frozen embeddings are about as linearly separable as the hand-built features, which is the standard test of what an encoder already knows.
  • Random forest is the weakest classifier on embeddings (0.839–0.878 against 0.892 for the baseline). PCA components spread the information over many dense features, which suits SVM and LogReg better than axis-aligned tree splits.
  • AgriFM is clearly behind (0.839–0.868; significantly worse with RF and SVM). Its input normalisation is still an open point, so this is not yet a fair verdict on the model.
  • The hardest test fold separates the models. In fold 0 (rainfed parcels in Doukkala and Souss), the baseline drops to 0.80 (RF, SVM) while Clay and Prithvi stay higher with every classifier (Prithvi 0.87 and Clay 0.86 with the SVM). Across the five folds Clay and Prithvi vary about as much as or less than the baseline (SD 0.045–0.054 with LogReg/SVM, vs 0.044–0.075 for the baseline).
  • Rainfed is the hard class: rainfed F1 ~0.81–0.84 for the best pairs against irrigated F1 ~0.97.

docs.title: Random versus spatial cross-validation
docs.text:
The same hyperparameters were re-evaluated with a stratified random 5-fold split that ignores the spatial blocks.

Input Classifier Random CV, mean macro-F1 Spatial CV, mean macro-F1 Spatial CV, worst fold S1/S2 baseline LogReg 0.904 0.895 0.847 S1/S2 baseline RF 0.928 0.893 0.804 S1/S2 baseline HGB 0.946 0.894 0.734 S1/S2 baseline SVM 0.926 0.911 0.830 Clay v1.5 SVM 0.936 0.911 0.844 Prithvi-EO-2.0 SVM 0.916 0.906 0.831 TerraMind SVM 0.933 0.903 0.802 AgriFM SVM 0.913 0.863 0.703

Random cross-validation is 1–5 points more optimistic for every input, and its folds lie within about one point of each other (SD ≤ 0.014), whereas the spatial folds differ by up to 0.24 (SD 0.04–0.10). Random validation thus both overstates accuracy and conceals the dependence of accuracy on the region.

Figure E01.1. Macro-F1 (left) and rainfed F1 (right) per fold for the S1/S2 baseline under random (grey) and spatial (blue) 5-fold cross-validation; bars mark the mean.

docs.title: What the baseline relies on
docs.text:
Grouped permutation importance of the random forest, computed on the test fold of each outer round: all features of one variable (or of one month) are permuted together and the drop in macro-F1 is recorded.

Variable Drop in macro-F1 Month Drop in macro-F1 NDWI 0.262 February 0.141 B12 (SWIR 2) 0.066 July 0.123 NDVI 0.046 August 0.113 EVI 0.026 June 0.091 B11 (SWIR 1) 0.013 October 0.089

Water-sensitive variables (NDWI, SWIR) dominate, and the most informative months are the peak of the rainfed season (February) and the dry summer (June–August), when only irrigated fields remain green. This supports the use of the full agricultural year. For the foundation-model embeddings, permuting a single month changes macro-F1 by at most 0.011 (Clay and Prithvi: February and May; TerraMind: July–September), i.e. the information is spread over the months.

Figure E01.2. Grouped permutation importance of the S1/S2 baseline (random forest) by variable (left) and by month (right); mean ± SD over the five outer folds.

The embeddings require strong regularisation of the linear probe (C = 0.01), whereas the baseline features prefer weaker regularisation. Class weighting and small trees are selected almost everywhere, and the SVM keeps its default setting for every foundation model.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: For RQ1, the frozen foundation models reach the accuracy of a conventional Sentinel-1/2 classifier but do not exceed it on average. This matches PANGAEA (Marsocci et al. 2024), where GeoFMs do not consistently beat supervised baselines. Where they may add value is robustness: in the region the baseline handles worst, Clay and Prithvi do better with every classifier. That points to the next questions: is this fold effect stable under the final validation design (E02), and does a learned temporal aggregation (E03) let the embeddings use the 12 months better than PCA?

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Nested validation design, replaced by the PASTIS rotation in E02; E01 is kept as a sensitivity check.
  • AgriFM normalisation not yet confirmed (open point in PROGRESS.md).
  • Small rainfed class (1,196 parcels, ~240 per fold): per-fold scores for rainfed rest on few parcels, hence the wide intervals.
  • Region and year are partly confounded (Gharb and Tadla only 2023/24; Souss only 2024/25), so the fold differences cannot be attributed to region alone.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Do frozen foundation-model embeddings separate irrigated from rainfed parcels better than Sentinel-1/2 features, with the same parcels, folds and classifiers, under the final validation design?

docs.title: Why
docs.text: E01 used nested spatial CV. The study now uses the PASTIS rotation for every model (classifiers and, later, neural networks), so they are trained, tuned and tested in exactly the same way (decision D3). E02 is the main result of RQ1; E01 becomes a sensitivity check of the validation design.

E01 E02 Validation nested: inner spatial CV on the 4 training folds, refit on all 4 PASTIS: 3 folds train, next fold validation, 1 fold test Model trained on 4 folds 3 folds

Inputs, embeddings, temporal aggregation (concat + PCA 128), classifiers, grids and metrics are unchanged; see the evaluation protocol.

docs.title: E03 · Frozen GeoFMs + L-TAE temporal aggregation
docs.text: Status 📝 planned — needs models_run/03c_train_ltae.py Research question RQ1 — how the monthly embeddings are combined Builds on E02 Config config.yaml

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Does a learned temporal aggregation of the 12 monthly embeddings (L-TAE) classify irrigated vs rainfed parcels better than concatenating the months and reducing them with PCA?

docs.title: Why
docs.text: Clay, Prithvi and TerraMind give one embedding per month. E01/E02 put the 12 months side by side and reduce them with PCA (a fixed, unsupervised step). PANGAEA (Marsocci et al. 2024) combines the monthly encodings of single-date models with a trained L-TAE and found it better than a linear mapping. E03 tests whether that holds for irrigated vs rainfed mapping. The same L-TAE is trained on the monthly S1/S2 features, so the baseline gets the same temporal model (protocol §5).

docs.title: What changes
docs.text:
E02 (PCA pipeline) E03 (L-TAE pipeline) Monthly embeddings → parcel vector concat 12 months → standardise → PCA 128 L-TAE attention over the 12 months (trained) Classifier LogReg, RF, HGB, SVM L-TAE output → small MLP head (trained together) Trained on 3 training folds 3 training folds; early stopping on the validation fold Inputs S1/S2, Clay, Prithvi, TerraMind, AgriFM S1/S2, Clay, Prithvi, TerraMind (AgriFM has no months) Seeds 1 (deterministic classifiers) 3 (neural network: mean ± SD over seeds)

The comparison step also reads the E02 runs (EXTRA_RUNS), so PCA and L-TAE are compared on the same parcels with the same bootstrap draws.

docs.title: Implementation plan (models_run/03c_train_ltae.py)
docs.text:
1. Read the same embedding files as 03_train_evaluate.py (<model>_agyear_tiles.npz, 12 steps × D) or the monthly S1/S2 features (17 variables × 12 months).
  2. Standardise per channel on the training folds; empty months are masked in the attention, not filled.
  3. L-TAE (Garnot & Landrieu 2020) with the paper's default size (16 heads, d_k 8, d_model 256, MLP 256-128), then an MLP head with 2 outputs; class-weighted cross-entropy.
  4. PASTIS rotation: train on 3 folds, early stopping on the validation fold (macro-F1), test on the test fold.
  5. Write oof_predictions.csv, metrics_per_fold.csv, metrics_with_ci.csv, run_config.json in the same format as script 03, with model = "ltae", so 04_compare_models.py and make_report.py work unchanged.

docs.title: ML-ready dataset (Morocco)
docs.text:
This page describes the construction of the machine-learning-ready dataset: labelled parcels, spatial train / validation / test folds, a common store of monthly Sentinel-1/2 imagery with label rasters, and derived views for the different model families.

Contents

  1. Overview
  2. Design principles
  3. Source data
  4. Script 01 — labels
  5. Script 02 — spatial folds
  6. Script 03 — tile store
  7. Script 04 — model views
  8. Output layout and file formats
  9. How to use the dataset
  10. Running, settings and run time
  11. Known limitations
  12. References

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
flowchart TD subgraph IN["Inputs"] FS["Field survey<br/>~10,000 parcels<br/>Dec 2023 – Jan 2025"] WC["ESA WorldCover 2021<br/>(cropland check)"] GEE["Google Earth Engine<br/>Sentinel-2 L2A · Cloud Score+<br/>Sentinel-1 GRD"] end FS --> S01["<b>01_prepare_labels.py</b><br/>clean geometry · label · cropland only<br/>agricultural year"] WC --> S01 S01 -->|"parcels_labelled.geojson<br/>8,781 parcels"| S02["<b>02_make_spatial_folds.py</b><br/>20 km blocks → 5 balanced folds"] S02 -->|"parcels_folds.geojson<br/>+ block_id, fold"| SPLIT[["Split by agricultural year<br/>(ag_season from survey date)"]] SPLIT -->|"2023/24 · 6,887 parcels<br/>imagery Sep 2023 – Aug 2024"| S03["<b>03_build_tiles.py</b><br/>run per agricultural year:<br/>128 × 128 px tiles · 12 months × 19 bands<br/>label / parcel-ID / edge rasters"] SPLIT -->|"2024/25 · 1,894 parcels<br/>imagery Sep 2024 – Aug 2025"| S03 GEE --> S03 S03 -->|"tiles/ · parcels.csv · tiles.parquet"| S04["<b>04_make_views.py</b><br/>cut every model input from the same pixels"] S04 --> VA["A · parcel feature tables<br/>(RF / boosting)"] S04 --> VB["B · pixel sets<br/>(PSE-TAE)"] S04 --> VC["C · patch-aligned chips<br/>chips_p8 · chips_p16<br/>(foundation models)"] S03 --> VD["D · full tiles<br/>(segmentation, U-TAE)"] Step Script What comes out 1 01_prepare_labels.py 8,781 labelled cropland parcels (7,585 irrigated, 1,196 rainfed) 2 02_make_spatial_folds.py a fold (0–4) per parcel, from 91 spatial blocks of 20 km 3 03_build_tiles.py the tile store: monthly images + label rasters + QA 4 04_make_views.py model inputs A–C (D = the tiles themselves)

Steps 1–2 complete within minutes. Step 3 requires several hours and resumes from the last completed tile when restarted. Step 4 runs locally.

docs.title: 2. Design principles
docs.text:
Principle How it is achieved One set of pixels for every model All imagery is downloaded once into one tile store. Every model input is cut from it locally, so differences between models cannot come from different compositing, masks or download windows. No duplicated downloads Fixed, non-overlapping 1.28 km tiles in one projection. Neighbouring parcels share tiles instead of each getting its own overlapping chip. Imagery matched to the label date Each parcel gets the 12 months of the agricultural year (1 Sep – 31 Aug) in which it was surveyed. The same place in another year is a different tile. Honest validation Folds are made of whole 20 km blocks, so a test parcel never has its next-door neighbour in training (section 5). Uncertain pixels kept, not dropped Label 0 = ignore (unlabelled or overlapping parcels), plus a separate edge flag for mixed boundary pixels. Users decide how to treat them. Documented quality Clear-observation counts per pixel and month, scene IDs per tile and month, QA per tile, overlap list, patch-purity scores. Patch-aware chips Chips for patch-based models are shifted so the parcel centroid sits at the centre of one model patch (section 7).

The layout follows existing ML-ready crop datasets. PASTIS (Garnot & Landrieu 2021) and Sen4AgriNet (Sykas et al. 2022) use fixed tiles with dense label and parcel-ID rasters. Fields of The World (Kerner et al. 2025) keeps an "unlabelled" ignore class. The ClarkCGA / Prithvi crop chips report QA counts per chip.

docs.title: 3. Source data
docs.text: Data Use Details Field survey (Ouassanouan et al. 2026, Scientific Data) labels ~10,000 parcel polygons, surveyed Dec 2023 – Jan 2025 in the Gharb, Tadla, Doukkala, El Haouz and Souss irrigation districts; land use, crop and irrigation method GADM 4.1 Morocco maps country outline ESA WorldCover 2021 (10 m) label check share of each parcel mapped as cropland Sentinel-2 L2A harmonised (COPERNICUS/S2_SR_HARMONIZED) imagery 12 bands, surface reflectance Cloud Score+ (GOOGLE/CLOUD_SCORE_PLUS/V1/S2_HARMONIZED) cloud mask cs_cdf ≥ 0.60 kept Sentinel-1 GRD (COPERNICUS/S1_GRD) imagery IW mode, VV + VH, ascending and descending kept apart

docs.title: 4. Script 01 — prepare_labels
docs.text:
Purpose: turn the raw survey into one clean file of labelled cropland parcels. Every later step starts from this file.

flowchart LR A["Survey shapefile"] --> B["Clean geometry<br/>drop empty · repair invalid<br/>drop exact duplicates"] B --> C["Normalise irrigation text<br/>(lower case, trimmed)"] C --> D{"Irrigation<br/>method?"} D -->|"drip · flood · sprinkler<br/>basin · pivot"| E["label 1<br/>irrigated"] D -->|"rainfed"| F["label 2<br/>rainfed"] D -->|"missing"| X["dropped"] E --> G{"Land use is<br/>cropland?"} F --> G G -->|"Seasonal Crop · Trees<br/>Trees + Seasonal"| H["Add attributes<br/>area_ha · ag_season<br/>nn_dist_m · WorldCover share"] G -->|"bare soil · weeds · water"| X H --> I["parcels_labelled.geojson<br/>summary.csv · figures"]

Steps

  1. Read the survey shapefile.
  2. Clean the geometry: drop parcels without geometry, repair invalid polygons, drop exact duplicates.
  3. Label it: any irrigation method (drip, flood, sprinkler, basin, pivot) = 1 irrigated; "rainfed" = 2 rainfed. Spelling variants are normalised.
  4. Keep cropland only: Seasonal Crop, Trees, Trees + Seasonal.
  5. Add these attributes:
  6. area_ha: area in UTM 29N.
  7. ag_season: agricultural year of the survey date (1 Sep – 31 Aug, e.g. 2023/24). This decides which imagery a parcel gets.
  8. nn_dist_m: distance to the nearest other parcel.
  9. wc_cropland_frac, wc_major: optional WorldCover check (CHECK_WORLDCOVER).
  10. Save the parcels, a summary table and four figures.

Result

Agricultural year Irrigated Rainfed Total 2023/24 6,189 (11,034 ha) 698 (836 ha) 6,887 2024/25 1,396 (2,020 ha) 498 (1,286 ha) 1,894 All 7,585 1,196 8,781

Median parcel size: 0.83 ha (10th–90th percentile: 0.30–3.5 ha). Rainfed parcels are 14% of the total, and nearly all of them (1,122 of 1,196) are in Doukkala. The classes are unbalanced, and the class is partly tied to the region, which is why section 5 matters.

Figure 1.1. Spatial distribution of the 8,781 labelled cropland parcels. Rainfed parcels are concentrated in Doukkala on the Atlantic coast. Figure 1.2. Class balance (left; 86.4% irrigated, 13.6% rainfed) and parcel-size distribution per class (right, logarithmic axis). Figure 1.3. Labelled parcels by survey month (December 2023 – January 2025). The survey date determines the agricultural year, and thus the imagery, assigned to each parcel.

docs.title: 5. Script 02 — make_spatial_folds
docs.text: Purpose: split the parcels into 5 folds so a model can be trained on some areas and tested on other areas. This is the dataset's train / validation / test split.

docs.title: 5.1 Why not a random split
docs.text: Surveyed parcels are typically a few hundred metres apart, and neighbouring parcels usually share a class. Under a random 5-fold split, 72% of test parcels have a training parcel within 250 m and 98% within 1 km. Accuracy then reflects the recognition of nearby parcels rather than the ability to map new areas, a bias documented by Roberts et al. (2017), Ploton et al. (2020) and Kattenborn et al. (2022).

docs.title: 5.2 Choosing the block size
docs.text:
The range of spatial dependence is estimated from the proportion of parcel pairs that share a class as a function of their distance. This proportion is compared with the random-placement level, i.e. the probability that two randomly drawn parcels share a class, 0.86² + 0.14² ≈ 76%. Beyond the distance at which the curve reaches this level, proximity carries no information about the class.

Distance between parcels 0.2 km 1 km 5 km 10 km 15 km 20 km 30 km 50 km Same class (%) 96.1 95.2 92.0 91.0 86.7 81.4 79.7 73.7 Figure 1.4. Proportion of parcel pairs sharing a class as a function of distance. The proportion approaches the random-placement level (76%, dashed) at about 20–30 km, which motivates the 20 km block size (dotted).

Candidate block sizes, each with 5 greedy-balanced folds:

Split Rainfed in smallest fold Rainfed share per fold Test parcels with a training parcel ≤ 250 m ≤ 1 km random 239 20–20% 79.4% 98.4% 2 km blocks 239 20–20% 12.8% 65.6% 5 km 239 20–20% 6.3% 31.7% 10 km 239 20–20% 3.2% 18.0% 20 km 238 20–20% 2.0% 10.2% 25 km 239 20–20% 1.8% 9.1% 30 km 142 12–34% 0.6% 4.6% 50 km 202 17–24% 1.2% 5.9%

20 km is the chosen size: - It is near the distance where class similarity approaches the random-placement level. - It cuts leakage to 2% at 250 m. - It still gives five folds with equal class shares.

From 30 km upwards there are too few blocks with rainfed parcels to balance the folds: one fold would hold 12% of the rainfed parcels and another 34%.

Resulting folds (whole blocks per fold):

Fold Irrigated Rainfed Blocks 0 1,528 239 12 1 1,528 239 13 2 1,473 241 42 3 1,528 238 11 4 1,528 239 13

Training parcel within … 100 m 250 m 500 m 1 km 5 km random split 24.1% 71.7% 90.1% 97.7% 99.7% 20 km spatial split 0.4% 1.8% 3.8% 8.1% 38.0% Figure 1.5. Fold assignment of the parcels (left) and class counts per fold (right). Each fold contains about 1,530 irrigated and 240 rainfed parcels. Figure 1.6. docs.title: 5.4 How the folds give train, validation and test
docs.text:
There is no single fixed train / validation / test split. The folds take turns, as in the PASTIS benchmark (Garnot & Landrieu 2021): in each of 5 rounds, 3 folds train, the next fold validates (chooses the hyperparameters) and one fold is the test fold.

Round Train Validation Test 1 folds 2, 3, 4 fold 1 fold 0 2 folds 3, 4, 0 fold 2 fold 1 3 folds 4, 0, 1 fold 3 fold 2 4 folds 0, 1, 2 fold 4 fold 3 5 folds 1, 2, 3 fold 0 fold 4

After 5 rounds every parcel has been tested once, by a model that never saw its block. Unlike PASTIS, the folds are made of whole 20 km blocks, so the test fold is always a set of regions the model has never seen.

For quick experiments, the column split gives one fixed split: fold 0 = test, fold 1 = validation, folds 2–4 = train. random_fold gives a stratified random split, so the optimism of random validation can be measured.

Outputs (outputs/dataset/02_folds/): - parcels_folds.geojson: parcels + block_id, fold, random_fold, split - fold_counts.csv - block_size_comparison.csv - class_similarity_by_distance.csv / .png - leakage_check.csv - spatial_folds.png, spatial_folds_blocks.png - train_test_distance.png

docs.title: 6. Script 03 — build_tiles
docs.text: Purpose: build the single image store that every model reads from.

docs.title: 6.1 Tile grid and which tiles are built
docs.text:
• One projection for the whole area, UTM 29N (EPSG:32629), with 10 m pixels. The few parcels in zone 30N are resampled.
  • A fixed grid of 128 × 128-pixel tiles (1.28 km × 1.28 km). Tile IDs are <season>_<ix>_<iy>, e.g. 2023-24_412_3561.
  • Only the tiles the parcels need are built:
  • home tile: holds the parcel centroid;
  • outline tiles: touched by the parcel polygon;
  • context tiles: reached by the largest model chip around the centroid. That is 64 px plus up to 8 px of alignment shift, i.e. 40 px (400 m) in every direction.
flowchart LR P["Parcel<br/>centroid + outline"] --> H["home tile<br/>(contains centroid)"] P --> O["outline tiles<br/>(polygon crosses into them)"] P --> C["context tiles<br/>(within 32 + 8 px of the centroid)"] H --> U["Union over all parcels<br/>and both seasons"] O --> U C --> U U --> T["Tile plan:<br/>each tile built once"]

docs.title: 6.2 Two agricultural years
docs.text:
The survey ran from December 2023 to January 2025, so the parcels belong to two agricultural years. Each parcel must be described by the imagery of the season in which its label was observed. A field that was irrigated in 2023/24 may be rainfed or fallow in 2024/25. The two years are therefore handled as two separate, parallel tile stores that share one grid:

flowchart TD A["Survey date of each parcel"] --> B["<b>ag_season</b> = agricultural year (1 Sep – 31 Aug)<br/>Sep–Dec of Y → Y/Y+1 · Jan–Aug of Y → Y−1/Y"] B --> P1["<b>2023/24</b> · 6,887 parcels<br/>tile plan: tile_id = 2023-24_ix_iy"] B --> P2["<b>2024/25</b> · 1,894 parcels<br/>tile plan: tile_id = 2024-25_ix_iy"] P1 --> X1["Label rasters: only 2023/24 parcels<br/>Earth Engine image Sep 2023 – Aug 2024<br/>(2023/24 tiles + 2 km)"] P2 --> X2["Label rasters: only 2024/25 parcels<br/>Earth Engine image Sep 2024 – Aug 2025<br/>(2024/25 tiles + 2 km)"] X1 --> T1["2,183 tiles (2023/24)"] X2 --> T2["804 tiles (2024/25)"] T1 --> S["One folder tiles/, one grid (same ix, iy),<br/>season in every tile name"] T2 --> S S --> V["04_make_views.py reads each parcel<br/>from the tiles of its own season"]

How each part of the pipeline handles the season:

Where How the season is handled 01_prepare_labels.py ag_season from the survey date: 1 Sep – 31 Aug (a parcel surveyed in Jan 2024 → 2023/24; Dec 2024 → 2024/25) Tile plan a tile is the triple (season, ix, iy). The same 1.28 km square can exist once for each year, with the same grid position. Tile name the season comes first: 2023-24_374_2793, 2024-25_374_2793 Label rasters only parcels of the tile's own year are burnt in, so a 2024/25 parcel never appears as a label in a 2023/24 tile Imagery one 12-month Earth Engine image per year, built over that year's tiles only. The month bands are named identically (m01 … m12), so both years have the same 228-band layout and models can mix them. QA, tiles.parquet one row per (season, tile), with an ag_season column Views (04_make_views.py) every parcel is cut from the tiles of its own season; ag_season is kept in every output table Folds (02) blocks are defined by location only, so a place surveyed in both years falls in the same block and fold. No information leaks between years from training to test. Viewing (tools/a4_build_vrt.py) one virtual raster per year, because the two years overlap in space

Currently 47 tile positions exist in both years: places with parcels surveyed in 2023/24 and in 2024/25.

Why the agricultural year (September – August).

gantt dateFormat YYYY-MM-DD axisFormat %b section Rainfed cereals Pre-season :r0, 2023-09-01, 2023-11-01 Sowing :r1, 2023-11-01, 2024-01-01 Growth, flowering Mar–Apr :r2, 2024-01-01, 2024-05-01 Harvest :r3, 2024-05-01, 2024-07-31 section Irrigated land Green whenever water is applied :i1, 2023-09-01, 2024-06-01 Dry summer :crit, i2, 2024-06-01, 2024-08-31 Reason Explanation One complete rainfed cycle rainfed cereals are sown in November–December and harvested in May–July; a calendar year would divide the cycle The dry summer carries the signal from June to August only irrigated fields remain green, the clearest contrast between the classes (confirmed by the permutation importance in E01) Irrigation status is seasonal rainfall, reservoir allocations and fallowing change which fields are irrigated, so a label is valid for one season Consistency with existing products LGRIP30, WorldCereal and GMIA-NEXT define irrigation for one growing season (Teluguntla et al., 2023; Van Tricht et al., 2023; Kebede et al., 2026) National convention the Moroccan agricultural campaign, including the accounting of seasonal rainfall, starts on 1 September

docs.title: 6.3 Monthly composites (per tile, per month)
docs.text:
flowchart TD subgraph S2["Sentinel-2 L2A"] direction TB A1["Scenes with cloud cover < 60 %"] --> A2["Cloud Score+ mask:<br/>keep pixels with cs_cdf ≥ 0.60"] A2 --> A3["Median of clear pixels<br/>12 bands, reflectance × 10,000"] A3 --> A4["+ S2_NCLEAR: number of<br/>clear observations"] end subgraph S1["Sentinel-1 GRD (IW, VV + VH)"] direction TB B1["Split by orbit:<br/>ascending / descending"] --> B2["dB → linear power;<br/>monthly mean"] B2 --> B3["→ dB × 100<br/>VV, VH per orbit"] B3 --> B4["+ S1_N: number of scenes"] end A4 --> M["One month = 19 bands"] B4 --> M M --> Y["12 months (Sep → Aug) = 228 bands, int16<br/>NODATA = −32768 where no observation"]
  • 19 bands per month:
  • B1, B2, B3, B4, B5, B6, B7, B8, B8A, B9, B11, B12
  • S2_NCLEAR
  • VV_ASC, VH_ASC, S1_N_ASC
  • VV_DSC, VH_DSC, S1_N_DSC
  • Months: m01 = September … m12 = August of the parcel's agricultural year. Band names in the GeoTIFF look like B4_m03 (red, November).
  • Why linear power for Sentinel-1: backscatter in dB is a logarithm. Averaging in dB gives the geometric mean and biases the composite downwards. Averaging is therefore done in linear power, and the result converted back to dB.
  • Why the orbits are kept apart: ascending and descending passes look at a field from different incidence angles, so their backscatter is not interchangeable. Both are stored, and the view script picks one.
  • Each tile's _scenes.json lists the Sentinel-1/2 scene IDs used in each month, so every pixel can be traced to its source.

docs.title: 6.4 Label rasters (local, no Earth Engine)
docs.text:
Each tile has a 3-band int32 label raster on exactly the same grid:

Band Values Meaning label 0 / 1 / 2 0 = unlabelled or ignore, 1 = irrigated, 2 = rainfed parcel_idx 0 / 1…N 0 = no parcel, otherwise the parcel's row in parcels.csv edge 0 / 1 1 = parcel pixel within 10 m of the outline (mixed boundary pixel)

Rules:

flowchart TD A["Parcel polygon<br/>(same season as the tile)"] --> B{"Contains at least<br/>one pixel centre?"} B -->|yes| C["Burn pixels whose<br/>centre is inside"] B -->|no: very small parcel| D["Burn all touched pixels<br/>flag all_touched = True"] C --> E{"Pixel claimed by<br/>two parcels?"} D --> E E -->|yes| F["label = 0, parcel_idx = 0<br/>(ignore) · pair listed in parcel_overlaps.csv"] E -->|no| G["label, parcel_idx set"] G --> H["edge = 1 if within 10 m<br/>of the outline"]

Only parcels of the tile's own agricultural year are burnt in.

docs.title: 6.5 Steps
docs.text:
1. Read the parcels with folds and project them to UTM 29N.
  2. Parcel table: index, centroid, bounds, area, perimeter, pixel counts (all and inner), home tile, tiles needed.
  3. Tile plan (6.1).
  4. Label rasters for all planned tiles (6.3). Local and fast.
  5. Earth Engine: one 228-band monthly image per agricultural year. Each tile is downloaded with computePixels, 8 requests in parallel and up to 4 retries, and written as a compressed GeoTIFF with its scene IDs. Finished tiles are skipped on a restart.
  6. Tile index (tiles.parquet) with fold, role, labelled pixels and QA.

DOWNLOAD = False stops after step 4, so the plan and labels can be checked without Earth Engine. N_TEST_TILES = 20 builds only 20 tiles per season, for a test run.

docs.title: 6.6 Quality numbers per tile
docs.text:
Column Meaning s2_nodata_pct share of tile-months without any clear Sentinel-2 pixel s2_nodata_parcel_pct the same, on parcel pixels only s2_nclear_parcel_median median number of clear observations on parcel pixels, per month s1_asc_months, s1_dsc_months months with at least one ascending / descending scene role home, outline or context mixed_folds the tile holds parcels from more than one fold (relevant for segmentation, section 11)

Outputs (outputs/dataset/03_tiles_128px/agyear/): - tiles/<id>_img.tif, tiles/<id>_lab.tif, tiles/<id>_scenes.json - parcels.csv - parcel_overlaps.csv - tiles.parquet - tiles_qa.jsonl - tiles_info.json

docs.title: 7. Script 04 — make_views
docs.text:
Purpose: cut every model input from the tile store. It runs locally and needs no Earth Engine.

flowchart TD TS["<b>Tile store</b><br/>tiles read through a cache of 48 tiles"] --> L["<b>For each parcel</b><br/>read its window and its pixels<br/>(label raster: parcel_idx = this parcel)"] L --> A["<b>View A · parcel features</b><br/>median per band and month + NDVI, NDWI, EVI<br/>parcel_features_all.csv · parcel_features_inner.csv"] L --> B["<b>View B · pixel sets</b><br/>all parcel pixels, all months<br/>pixelsets.npz"] L --> C["<b>View C · 64 × 64 chips</b><br/>patch-aligned, per patch size<br/>chips_p8/ (Clay) · chips_p16/ (others)"] TS --> D["<b>View D · full tiles</b><br/>as they are, for<br/>segmentation models"]

docs.title: 7.1 View A — parcel feature tables
docs.text:
• Per parcel and month: the median over the parcel's pixels of each of these:
  • the 12 Sentinel-2 bands (reflectance 0–1);
  • NDVI = (B8 − B4)/(B8 + B4);
  • NDWI = (B8 − B11)/(B8 + B11), which measures canopy water;
  • EVI = 2.5 (B8 − B4)/(B8 + 6 B4 − 7.5 B2 + 1);
  • VV and VH for both orbits (dB).
  • Indices are computed per pixel first, then the median is taken.
  • The median is used instead of the mean because it is robust to leftover clouds and mixed edge pixels.
  • Observation counts are added: the mean S2_NCLEAR over the parcel, and the maximum S1_N per orbit.
  • Column names are <variable>_m<month>, e.g. NDVI_m10 (NDVI in June). Each parcel has 19 variables × 12 months = 228 feature columns, plus counts and metadata (parcel_id, label, ag_season, fold, n_px_used, used_inner).
  • parcel_features_inner.csv leaves out edge pixels. A parcel with no inner pixel falls back to all of its pixels (used_inner = False).

docs.title: 7.2 View B — pixel sets
docs.text:
All pixels of each parcel, unaggregated, for set-based temporal models such as PSE-TAE (Garnot et al. 2020).

  • pixels [N_pixels, 12, bands] int16
  • offsets [parcels + 1]: parcel i = pixels[offsets[i]:offsets[i+1]]
  • edge [N_pixels], parcel_id, label, bands

docs.title: 7.3 View C — patch-aligned chips for the foundation models
docs.text:
Vision-transformer foundation models partition an image into square patches: 8 × 8 px for Clay and 16 × 16 px (160 m) for Prithvi-EO-2.0, TerraMind and the output grid of AgriFM. Each patch is represented by one embedding.

When a chip whose size is a multiple of the patch size is centred on the parcel, the centroid falls on the corner of four patches, and a small parcel is distributed over four patches dominated by neighbouring fields. Shifting the chip by half a patch places the centroid at the centre of a single patch:

flowchart LR subgraph OLD["Centred chip (old)"] O1["Centroid on the corner<br/>of 4 patches"] --> O2["Parcel split over 4 patches,<br/>each mostly neighbouring fields"] end subgraph NEW["Patch-aligned chip (now)"] N1["Chip shifted by half a patch<br/>(4 px for p8, 8 px for p16)"] --> N2["Centroid at the centre<br/>of one patch"] N2 --> N3["Higher share of the pooled<br/>patches inside the parcel"] end OLD -.->|"replaced by"| NEW

Purity measures this. A patch's weight is the share of its pixels inside the parcel, and those weights are also what the study uses to pool patch embeddings. Purity is the weighted share of parcel pixels in the pooled patches: Σ w² / Σ w, from 0 to 1. index.csv stores both purity (aligned) and purity_centred (old rule), so the gain is measurable.

Each chip folder holds: - part_*.npz: chips [n, 12, 15, 64, 64] int16, mask [n, 64, 64] (parcel pixels), parcel_id. - index.csv: one row per parcel. Columns: part, label, ag_season, fold, zone, lat, lon, epsg, x0, y0 (chip top-left corner, for georeferencing), area_ha, n_px, n_px_in_chip, purity, purity_centred. - chips_info.json: band order and scales. The 15 bands are B1 … B12, VV, VH, S2_NCLEAR.

Figure 1.8. Patch purity, i.e. the share of the pooled patches that lies inside the parcel, for centred chips (grey) and patch-aligned chips (blue), at 8 px (80 m, left) and 16 px (160 m, right) patch size. Alignment markedly increases purity, in particular for 8 px patches.

docs.title: 7.4 Sentinel-1 orbit for views B and C
docs.text: S1_ORBIT = "auto" picks the orbit direction with more valid tile-months over the whole study area and writes it to views_info.json (s1_orbit_for_chips_and_pixelsets). That orbit's bands are named simply VV and VH in the chips. "ASC" or "DSC" force one orbit. View A keeps both orbits as separate columns.

docs.title: 7.5 QA files
docs.text:
• qa_clear_obs.csv: clear observations per parcel and month.
  • qa_purity.csv: purity distribution per patch size.
  • views_info.json: settings, the chosen orbit, and counts.

docs.title: 7.6 Dataset inspection
docs.text:
The checks of models_run/01_inspect_dataset.py (Model training and inference §4) characterise the final dataset before any model is trained.

Figure 1.9. Mean number of clear Sentinel-2 observations per parcel and month (left) and share of parcels without any clear observation (right). Winter months have the fewest clear views, yet every parcel has at least one clear observation in every month. Figure 1.10. Monthly parcel medians of NDVI, NDWI and Sentinel-1 VH backscatter (median and interquartile range per class). Irrigated parcels show markedly higher vegetation and moisture signals from December to April and higher backscatter throughout the year; rainfed parcels show a weak, short spring peak. Figure 1.11. Example irrigated parcels: 16 px-aligned chips for the 12 months of the agricultural year, in true colour and NDVI (outline = parcel). Figure 1.12. Example rainfed parcels, displayed as in Figure 1.11.

docs.title: 11. Known limitations
docs.text:
• Class balance and geography: 14% of parcels are rainfed, and 94% of those are in Doukkala. A model can partly learn "region" rather than "irrigation". Per-zone results should be reported.
  • Reprojection: the few parcels in UTM 30N are resampled to 29N.
  • Monthly composites: in cloudy winter months some parcels have no clear Sentinel-2 view (NODATA). The counts show where.
  • Segmentation with view D: a tile can hold parcels of two folds (mixed_folds), and context tiles reach across fold borders. Tile-level models need their own tile split, or a loss mask restricted to the training fold.
  • Labels: a single survey visit per parcel. Overlapping parcels are set to ignore and listed, but labels are not otherwise checked against imagery.

docs.title: Evaluation protocol
docs.text:
This protocol defines the rules common to all experiments and ensures that results are comparable across inputs, classifiers and experiments. Any deviation must be declared in the experiment's What changes table.

Contents: 1 Task · 2 Splits · 3 Inputs · 4 Classifiers · 5 Temporal aggregation · 6 Fairness rules · 7 Metrics · 8 Reading a result · 9 Reporting · References

docs.title: 1. Task and unit
docs.text: The task is binary classification of parcels into irrigated (class 1) and rainfed (class 2), with one label and one prediction per surveyed parcel; all metrics are computed at parcel level. 8,781 parcels (7,585 irrigated, 1,196 rainfed); inputs are scored on the parcels present in every run (8,775: six parcels fully covered by overlapping polygons have no own pixel).

docs.title: 2. Spatial splits
docs.text:
Parcels are grouped into 20 km blocks, and the blocks into 5 folds with the same class balance (about 1,530 irrigated and 240 rainfed parcels each). A block is never split. A place surveyed in both seasons stays in one fold. Block size and fold assignment: dataset §5.

Main design: PASTIS rotation (Garnot & Landrieu 2021). Five rounds; in each, 3 folds train, the next fold is the validation fold, one fold is the test fold:

Round Train Validation (choose settings / early stopping) Test 1 2, 3, 4 1 0 2 3, 4, 0 2 1 3 4, 0, 1 3 2 4 0, 1, 2 4 3 5 1, 2, 3 0 4

The model is trained on the 3 training folds with the setting that scored best on the validation fold. The test fold is never used for any choice. After 5 rounds every parcel has one out-of-fold prediction from a model that never saw its block. Classifiers and neural networks use the same rotation.

Why a rotation rather than one fixed split. (i) Every parcel is tested once, so the rainfed scores rest on all 1,196 rainfed parcels instead of the ~240 of a single test fold. (ii) Five different test areas reveal how strongly accuracy depends on the region, which a single test area would show only by chance. (iii) Hyperparameters are never chosen on the test fold, so the reported accuracy is not inflated by tuning (Varma & Simon, 2006). The same principle of spatially separated folds is implemented in blockCV (Valavi et al., 2019) and used for crop-type classification with Sentinel-1/2 by Orynbaikyzy et al. (2022); Schratz et al. (2019) recommend spatial folds for tuning as well as for testing.

Sensitivity design: nested spatial CV (VALIDATION: nested, experiment E01): settings chosen by spatial CV on the 4 non-test folds, model refit on all 4.

Random CV (stratified, ignoring blocks) is only used inside a run to show how much it overstates accuracy.

docs.title: 3. Inputs
docs.text: Five inputs are compared: a Sentinel-1/2 parcel-feature baseline (12 Sentinel-2 bands, NDVI, NDWI, EVI and Sentinel-1 VV, VH over 12 months; 204 features) and the embeddings of four frozen foundation models (Clay v1.5, Prithvi-EO-2.0, TerraMind, AgriFM). A parcel's embedding is the mean of the patch embeddings that cover it, weighted by the share of each patch inside the parcel; chips are 64 × 64 px and shifted so that the parcel centroid lies at a patch centre. Bands, patch size and temporal handling per model: Foundation models · Configuration.

docs.title: 4. Classifiers
docs.text:
Classifier Grid (chosen on the validation fold, by macro-F1) Fixed logreg logistic regression (linear probe) C ∈ balanced classes, standardised rf random forest max_features ∈ {√p, 0.3} · min_samples_leaf ∈ {1, 5} · class_weight ∈ {none, balanced_subsample} 500 trees hgb histogram gradient boosting learning_rate ∈ {0.05, 0.1} · max_leaf_nodes ∈ {15, 31} · class_weight ∈ {none, balanced} svm RBF support vector machine C ∈ {1, 10} · γ ∈ {scale, 0.01} balanced classes, standardised

Headline classifiers: random forest (the proposal's baseline classifier) for every input, and logistic regression (linear probe) for the foundation models. HGB and SVM are robustness checks and are always reported.

docs.title: 5. Temporal aggregation: two pipelines
docs.text:
How the 12 monthly embeddings of a parcel become one input for the classifier is the step that differs between the two pipelines. Everything before (embeddings) and after (comparison, metrics) is shared.

flowchart LR E["<b>Monthly embeddings</b><br/>12 × D per parcel<br/>(AgriFM: 1 × D)"] --> A["<b>PCA pipeline</b><br/>fill empty months (training median)<br/>→ concat 12 months → standardise<br/>→ PCA 128, fitted on the training folds"] E --> B["<b>L-TAE pipeline</b><br/>standardise per channel<br/>→ L-TAE attention over the months<br/>(empty months masked)"] A --> C["LogReg · RF · HGB · SVM<br/>grid on the validation fold"] B --> D["MLP head, trained with the L-TAE<br/>early stopping on the validation fold<br/>3 seeds"] C --> O["<b>oof_predictions.csv</b><br/>same format"] D --> O O --> CMP["compare: same parcels,<br/>same bootstrap draws"] PCA pipeline L-TAE pipeline Experiments E01, E02 E03 Learns which months matter no (PCA is unsupervised) yes (attention weights) Keeps the order of the months only as positions in the vector yes (positional encoding) Classifier the four of §4 its own MLP head Applies to the baseline yes (204 features, no PCA) yes (17 variables × 12 months) Applies to AgriFM yes no (one vector per year) Reference linear probing of frozen features PANGAEA: single-date encoders + L-TAE (Marsocci et al. 2024); L-TAE (Garnot & Landrieu 2020)

The L-TAE pipeline is also trained on the monthly S1/S2 features, so that the baseline benefits from the same temporal model and the comparison remains balanced. Because both pipelines write the same out-of-fold predictions, E03 compares them directly with the E02 runs on the same parcels.

docs.title: 6. Fairness rules
docs.text:
flowchart LR subgraph SAME["Identical for every input"] P1["same parcels<br/>(common to all runs)"] P2["same pixels<br/>(one tile store)"] P3["same folds<br/>and rotation"] P4["same classifiers<br/>and grids"] P5["same metrics and<br/>bootstrap draws"] end SAME --> D["only the input<br/>(or the one setting the<br/>experiment varies) differs"] D --> C["paired difference<br/>with 95% CI"]
  1. Every fitted step (imputation, standardisation, PCA, tuning, early stopping) uses the training folds only; the validation fold only chooses settings; the test fold is used once, for the prediction.
  2. All inputs come from the same tile store: same composites, cloud mask, months and parcels.
  3. Settings are chosen with the same budget for every input (the grids above).
  4. Inputs are compared on the parcels common to all runs, with the same bootstrap draws.
  5. An experiment varies one thing against the experiment it builds on, and says so in its README.

docs.title: 7. Metrics and uncertainty
docs.text:
Metric Role Macro-F1 headline: mean of irrigated F1 and rainfed F1, so the 14% rainfed class counts equally F1, precision, recall per class rainfed recall: how many rainfed fields are found Balanced accuracy mean recall of both classes Overall accuracy for comparison with the literature (predicting "all irrigated" already gives 86%) PR-AUC (rainfed), Brier score, ECE ranking quality and calibration of the predicted probabilities Macro-F1 per fold, mean ± SD stability across regions (the proposal's selection criterion)

The kappa coefficient is not reported, as it is uninformative for accuracy assessment (Pontius & Millones, 2011).

95% confidence intervals: block bootstrap (Künsch, 1989). The 91 blocks, not the parcels, are the independent units. Each of 1,000 draws resamples whole blocks with replacement and recomputes the metric; the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles give the interval. The same 1,000 draws are used for every run, so a difference between two inputs is measured on identical resamples (paired).

docs.title: 8. How a result is read
docs.text:
• Δ macro-F1 = input − baseline, with the same classifier (runs with their own model, such as L-TAE or PSE-TAE, against the baseline random forest).
  • An input is better (or worse) than the baseline only if the 95% CI of Δ excludes 0 and the Holm-adjusted p-value is below 0.05. Holm corrects for testing all inputs × classifiers together.
  • A CI that excludes 0 without surviving Holm is reported as "higher / lower, not significant after Holm".
  • Otherwise: no clear difference. With ~240 rainfed parcels per fold, differences below about 0.02 macro-F1 are usually inside the noise.

docs.title: 9. Reporting standard
docs.text: Every experiment has a report page (docs/experiments/<name>/report.md) with, in this order: the answer in one or two sentences, the key findings, the setup, the result tables and figures (generated by experiments/make_report.py from the results), the interpretation, the caveats and the next steps. A finished experiment adds a one-line answer to its config.yaml, which appears on the Results page.

docs.title: RQ2 · Fine-tuning and mapping model
docs.text:
Starter page

Design as planned; extended when the work begins (planned November 2026 – January 2027).

Research question RQ2: to what extent does parameter-efficient fine-tuning improve on a frozen encoder?

docs.title: Planned design
docs.text:
The frozen-encoder benchmark of RQ1 pools embeddings over parcel polygons and cannot produce wall-to-wall maps. RQ2 therefore introduces a pixel-level model that serves both as the fine-tuning experiment and as the mapping model of Phase 5 (decision D11).

Component Description Frozen encoder + segmentation head each GeoFM with a UPerNet head trained on the labelled pixels of the tiles, as in PANGAEA and Prithvi-EO-2.0 Parameter-efficient fine-tuning low-rank adaptation (LoRA) of the encoder with the same head Full fine-tuning (optional) all encoder weights trained, for the best model only Classical baseline random forest on the per-pixel Sentinel-1/2 features Neural baselines TempCNN (per-pixel time series) and U-TAE (image time series), trained from scratch

Training, tuning and testing follow the evaluation protocol: the same spatial folds and the PASTIS rotation. Pixel predictions are additionally aggregated to parcels, so that the results are directly comparable with RQ1.
