docs.title: RQ1 · Frozen encoders: embeddings and classifiers
docs.text:
This page documents the frozen-encoder evaluation of Phase 2 (RQ1), which tests whether frozen embeddings of geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs) discriminate irrigated from rainfed cropland parcels in Morocco better than a conventional Sentinel-1/2 feature baseline under an identical spatial validation design.

It reads only the ML-ready dataset produced in ml_dataset_prep/. The rules of the comparison are summarised in the evaluation protocol; reported results are produced as experiments, which run these scripts with the settings of a config file.

Contents

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
The workflow below leads from the ML-ready dataset of Phase 1 to the final comparison: the five inputs (feature baseline and four frozen foundation models), the classifiers and their tuning grids, the spatial validation and the paired comparison.

flowchart TD FA["<b>Parcel features</b><br/>median of inner pixels"] C8["<b>Chips p8</b><br/>64 × 64 px, 8-px patches"] C16["<b>Chips p16</b><br/>64 × 64 px, 16-px patches"] FO["<b>Spatial folds</b><br/>20 km blocks"] FA --> B0["<b>S1/S2 baseline</b><br/>204 features"] C8 --> B1["<b>Clay v1.5</b><br/>12 × 1024"] C16 --> B2["<b>Prithvi-EO-2.0</b><br/>12 × 1024"] C16 --> B3["<b>TerraMind</b><br/>12 × 768"] C16 --> B4["<b>AgriFM</b><br/>1 × D"] B1 --> POOL["<b>Frozen encoder → parcel embedding</b><br/>patch-share-weighted mean over the parcel<br/>months side by side → standardise → PCA 128<br/>(fitted on the training folds only)"] B2 --> POOL B3 --> POOL B4 --> POOL B0 --> HUB["<b>03 · train and evaluate</b><br/>LogReg (linear probe) · RF · HGB · SVM<br/>same grids for every input"] POOL --> HUB HUB --> CV["<b>Spatial CV, 5 rounds</b> (PASTIS scheme)<br/>3 folds train · next fold validation · 1 fold test"] FO -. Step Script GPU What it does 1 01_inspect_dataset.py no checks the dataset before any model is trained 2 02a_embed_clay.py … 02d_embed_agrifm.py recommended frozen GeoFM embeddings per parcel 3 03_train_evaluate.py no trains and evaluates the classifiers for one input (run once per input) 4 04_compare_models.py no compares all inputs on the same parcels

docs.title: 2. Research questions and design
docs.text:
1. Main: does a frozen GeoFM embedding classify irrigated vs rainfed parcels better than Sentinel-1/2 parcel features, when tested on areas the model has never seen?
  2. Which GeoFM works best, and does the classifier on top matter?
  3. How much does random cross-validation overstate accuracy compared with spatial cross-validation?
  4. Which months (and, for the baseline, which variables) carry the signal?

The design keeps everything equal except the input:

flowchart LR SAME["<b>Kept identical for every input</b><br/>same parcels (intersection of all runs)<br/>same pixels (one tile store)<br/>same spatial folds (20 km blocks)<br/>same 4 classifiers and grids<br/>same metrics and bootstrap samples"] --> D["<b>Only the input differs</b><br/>S1/S2 features vs<br/>Clay · Prithvi · TerraMind · AgriFM"] D --> C["<b>Paired difference</b><br/>in macro-F1 with<br/>95% block-bootstrap CI"]

The foundation models are used frozen, as fixed feature extractors, following the linear-probing protocol. No fine-tuning is performed at this stage; the evaluation therefore measures the information contained in the pretrained representations, at low computational cost and under identical conditions for all inputs.

docs.title: 3. Inputs compared
docs.text: The five inputs (S1/S2 baseline and four frozen GeoFMs), their bands, patch sizes and temporal handling, and the sensitivity runs that isolate the Sentinel-1 contribution are specified in Foundation models · Configuration.

docs.title: 4. Script 01 — inspect_dataset
docs.text:
Purpose: find problems in the data before they show up as strange model results. It reads the dataset only and changes nothing.

flowchart LR IN["<b>Dataset files</b><br/>parcels · tiles · overlaps<br/>parcel features · chips · views_info"] --> S["<b>Seven checks</b><br/>1 · inventory per class, season, fold<br/>2 · label QA: overlaps, tiny parcels<br/>3 · observations per month (S2, S1)<br/>4 · patch purity, aligned vs centred<br/>5 · seasonal profiles per class<br/>6 · example chips, 12 months<br/>7 · agreement with the old NDVI table"] S --> OUT["outputs/study/<br/>01_inspection/"]

What to look for: - Inventory: all 8,781 parcels should reach view A and both chip folders. Missing parcels point to tiles that failed to download. - Observations: winter months (Dec–Feb) have the fewest clear Sentinel-2 views. If a month is empty for most parcels, its features carry little information. - Purity: the aligned chips should have a clearly higher median purity than the centred chips, especially for 16-px patches and small parcels. - Profiles: rainfed parcels should peak in winter (around February) and be bare from May. Irrigated parcels should stay green, or green up again, in summer. This is the signal every model should find. - Legacy agreement: high per-month correlation with the old Earth Engine NDVI confirms the new compositing. The old table used 30-day periods rather than calendar months, so the numbers will not be identical.

Outputs: - inventory.csv - label_qa.csv - observations_per_month.csv / .png - purity_summary.csv, purity.png - seasonal_profiles.png - examples_irrigated.png, examples_rainfed.png - legacy_agreement.csv

The resulting figures are shown in Dataset preparation §7.6.

For a closer look in QGIS, tools/a3_export_chips_geotiff.py writes single chips as georeferenced GeoTIFFs to 01_inspection/chips_geotiff/.

docs.title: 5. Scripts 02a–02d — foundation-model embeddings
docs.text:
All four scripts follow the same pattern. Only the model, its bands and its normalisation change.

flowchart TD A["Chip of one parcel<br/>12 months × 15 bands × 64 × 64 px<br/>+ parcel mask"] --> B["Select the bands the model<br/>was pretrained on"] B --> C["Normalise with the model's own<br/>pretraining mean / std<br/>NODATA (cloud) → 0 = band mean"] C --> D["Frozen encoder<br/>(no gradient, eval mode)"] D --> E["Patch tokens on their grid<br/>8 × 8 (Clay) or 4 × 4 (others)"] A -->|"mask"| W["Patch weight = share of the<br/>patch's pixels inside the parcel"] E --> F["Weighted mean of the patches<br/>covering the parcel"] W --> F F --> G["One vector per month<br/>(AgriFM: one per year)"] G --> H["valid flag = month had<br/>any clear pixel"] G --> O["<model>_agyear_tiles.npz<br/>embeddings [N, steps, D] float16"] H --> O

Pooling. Each patch token is weighted by the share of its pixels inside the parcel. Patches without any parcel pixel get weight 0. The parcel embedding is the weighted mean, so it describes the parcel and not the whole 640 m chip. The patch-aligned chips (dataset §7.3) put most of the weight on one patch centred on the parcel.

Cloudy pixels. NODATA pixels are set to 0 after normalisation, which equals the band mean. A month with no clear pixel at all is flagged valid = False, and script 03 fills it with the training median.

Resume. Embeddings are saved in batches (_parts_<model>_agyear_tiles/) and merged at the end. A stopped run continues from the last batch.

docs.title: 6. Script 03 — train_evaluate
docs.text: Purpose: one script for every input, so all inputs are evaluated in exactly the same way. Set INPUT at the top and run it once per input.

docs.title: 6.1 From input to feature matrix
docs.text:
flowchart TD subgraph BASE["INPUT = s1s2 (baseline)"] A1["parcel_features_inner.csv"] --> A2["Drop bookkeeping and count columns<br/>keep one S1 orbit, renamed VV / VH"] A2 --> A3["Fill fully cloudy months by<br/>linear interpolation in time<br/>(per parcel, own values only)"] A3 --> A4["204 features<br/>17 variables × 12 months"] end subgraph EMB["INPUT = GeoFM"] B1["<model>_agyear_tiles.npz"] --> B2{"FEATURE_MODE"} B2 -->|"concat (default)"| B3["all months side by side<br/>e.g. 12 × 1024 = 12,288"] B2 -->|"mean"| B4["average over months"] end A4 --> J["Join with folds (parcels_folds.geojson)<br/>keep parcels present in both"] B3 --> J B4 --> J J --> X["X, y, fold, block_id"]

Preprocessing inside every model pipeline. It is fitted on the training folds only, so no information leaks from the test fold: - Baseline: median imputation of any remaining gap. - Embeddings: median imputation of empty months, then standardisation. In concat mode, PCA to 128 components follows.

docs.title: 6.2 Classifiers and hyperparameter grids
docs.text:
Name Classifier Principle Grid (chosen on the validation fold) Fixed settings logreg Logistic regression one linear decision boundary; on frozen embeddings the standard linear probe (Alain & Bengio, 2016), which measures the information contained in the features C ∈ L2 penalty, lbfgs, max_iter = 5000, class_weight = "balanced", standardised inputs rf Random forest (Breiman, 2001) vote of many decision trees, each grown on a bootstrap sample and random feature subsets; the usual classifier in irrigation mapping max_features ∈ {√p, 0.3}; min_samples_leaf ∈ {1, 5}; class_weight ∈ {none, balanced_subsample} 500 trees, no depth limit, seed 42 hgb Histogram gradient boosting small trees added sequentially, each correcting the previous errors; features binned into histograms learning_rate ∈ {0.05, 0.1}; max_leaf_nodes ∈ {15, 31}; class_weight ∈ {none, balanced} 300 boosting rounds; built-in early stopping off, because it would use a random rather than a spatial validation split svm RBF support vector machine maximum-margin boundary, made non-linear by the RBF kernel; used for irrigation mapping with Sentinel-1/2 (Gao et al., 2018; Elwan et al., 2022) C ∈ {1, 10}; γ ∈ {scale, 0.01} class_weight = "balanced", standardised inputs; no probability calibration (the decision score is used for PR-AUC)

The settings selected in each round are reported per experiment (E01).

The selection score is macro-F1, the mean of the irrigated F1 and rainfed F1. It treats the 14% rainfed class as equally important.

docs.title: 6.3 Spatial cross-validation: train / validation / test
docs.text:
Each round uses the 5 spatial folds in the same way as the PASTIS benchmark (Garnot & Landrieu 2021): 3 folds train, the next fold is the validation fold, and one fold is the test fold. Rotating through 5 rounds tests every fold once.

Round Train Validation Test 1 folds 2, 3, 4 fold 1 fold 0 2 folds 3, 4, 0 fold 2 fold 1 3 folds 4, 0, 1 fold 3 fold 2 4 folds 0, 1, 2 fold 4 fold 3 5 folds 1, 2, 3 fold 0 fold 4 flowchart TD START["5 spatial folds<br/>(20 km blocks)"] --> R{"Round k = 1 … 5"} R --> TE["Test = fold k<br/>held out completely"] R --> VA["Validation = next fold<br/>chooses the hyperparameters"] R --> TR["Train = the other 3 folds"] TR --> G["Train every setting of the grid"] G --> VA2["Score each setting on the validation fold (macro-F1)"] VA --> VA2 VA2 --> BEST["Best setting, trained on the 3 training folds"] BEST --> PRED["Predict test fold k<br/>(class + rainfed score)"] TE --> PRED PRED --> OOF["After 5 rounds: every parcel predicted once,<br/>by a model that never saw its block"] OOF --> MET["Metrics + 95% block-bootstrap CI"]

The validation fold is used only to choose the classifier's hyperparameters; the test fold is never used for any choice. The same scheme is used for every input, so the classifiers and a later neural-network baseline are trained, tuned and tested identically. VALIDATION = "nested" in 03_train_evaluate.py gives the alternative design (tuning by spatial CV on the 4 training folds, refit on all 4), for a sensitivity check; its runs get the suffix _nested.

Every parcel is predicted once, by a model that saw neither its block in training nor any information from it during tuning. That makes the score an estimate of how well the model maps new areas.

docs.title: 6.4 Metrics and uncertainty
docs.text:
Metric Why Macro-F1 (headline) balances both classes; insensitive to the 86 / 14 split F1, precision, recall per class rainfed recall shows how many rainfed parcels are found Balanced accuracy mean recall of both classes Overall accuracy for comparison with the literature; the trivial "all irrigated" model already gets 86% PR-AUC (rainfed) threshold-free ranking quality for the minority class Brier score, expected calibration error quality of the predicted probabilities

95% confidence intervals: block bootstrap. Parcels in one 20 km block are correlated, so blocks, not parcels, are the independent units. Each of the 1,000 draws resamples whole blocks with replacement and recomputes every metric. The 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles give the interval.

flowchart LR A["Out-of-fold predictions<br/>with block_id"] --> B["Draw 91 blocks<br/>with replacement"] B --> C["Recompute metrics on<br/>the parcels of those blocks"] C --> D{"1,000 draws?"} D -->|no| B D -->|yes| E["2.5% / 97.5% quantiles<br/>= 95% CI"]

docs.title: 6.5 Further analyses in the same run
docs.text:
1. Classifier comparison: paired macro-F1 differences between the 4 classifiers on the same parcels, with block-bootstrap CIs.
  2. Spatial vs random CV: the same hyperparameters re-evaluated with the stratified random_fold. The gap shows how much random validation overstates accuracy.
  3. Grouped permutation importance: uses the random forest of each outer fold, on its test fold. For the baseline it is computed by variable (NDVI, VH, …) and by month; for embeddings, by month.
  4. Seasonal profiles (baseline): class medians per variable and month.
  5. Final models: refit on all parcels (final_model_<name>.joblib), for mapping later.

Outputs (experiments/<EXPERIMENT>/results/<RUN_NAME>/ in experiment mode; outputs/study/03_models/<RUN_NAME>/ for development runs with EXPERIMENT = None): - metrics_summary.csv, metrics_with_ci.csv, metrics_per_fold.csv - paired_model_differences.csv - cv_random_vs_spatial.csv / .png - oof_predictions.csv - selected_hyperparameters.csv, inner_tuning_scores.csv - importance.csv / .png - confusion_matrices.png - seasonal_profiles.png, gap_filling.csv (baseline only) - final_model_*.joblib - run_config.json, run.log

Run names: - Baseline: s1s2-<variables>_agyear_tiles-<inner|all>-<orbit>, e.g. s1s2-all_agyear_tiles-inner-asc. - GeoFMs: <model>_agyear_tiles_<concat|mean>, e.g. clay_agyear_tiles_concat.

docs.title: 7. Script 04 — compare_models
docs.text:
Purpose: answer the main research question by comparing every input with the baseline, on the same parcels.

flowchart TD A["oof_predictions.csv<br/>of each run in RUNS"] --> B["Keep parcels predicted in ALL runs"] B --> C["One shared set of 1,000<br/>block-bootstrap samples"] C --> D["Per run × classifier:<br/>macro-F1, rainfed F1,<br/>balanced and overall accuracy, 95% CI"] C --> E["Per GeoFM run × classifier:<br/>Δ macro-F1 vs baseline (same classifier)<br/>95% CI + bootstrap p-value"] E --> F["Holm adjustment over<br/>all comparisons"] D --> OUT["metrics_all_runs.csv<br/>comparison_macro_f1.png"] F --> OUT2["differences_vs_baseline.csv<br/>differs = CI excludes 0"]
  • Paired: the same bootstrap blocks are used for every run, so each difference is measured on identical resamples (Foody 2009).
  • Multiple comparisons: 4 GeoFMs × 4 classifiers = 16 comparisons, Holm-adjusted.
  • Interpretation: a GeoFM is better than the baseline only if the 95% interval of Δ macro-F1 lies entirely above 0.

BASELINE_RUN must match the orbit that was actually used (views_info.json), for example s1s2-all_agyear_tiles-inner-asc.

docs.title: Phase 2 · Model evaluation
docs.text:
Phase 2 addresses Objective 1, the comparison of foundation models and adaptation strategies in Morocco, through two research questions. Both are evaluated on spatially independent areas under one evaluation protocol.

RQ Question Approach Status Page RQ1 What accuracy does each foundation model achieve, compared with a conventional Sentinel-based classifier? frozen encoders → parcel embeddings → classifiers, vs a Sentinel-1/2 feature baseline ⏳ E01 done, E02 running, E03 planned RQ1 · Frozen encoders RQ2 To what extent does parameter-efficient fine-tuning improve on a frozen encoder? segmentation head on frozen and LoRA-adapted encoders; neural baselines 📝 planned RQ2 · Fine-tuning

The remainder of this page summarises the RQ1 workflow, which forms the reference for all later comparisons.

Unit of analysis. Each parcel carries one label recorded in the field survey. Models predict this label from satellite time series alone and are evaluated exclusively on parcels located in areas excluded from training.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text: flowchart TD     subgraph P1["Phase 1 · Dataset"]         GT["<b>Ground data</b><br/>field-surveyed parcels (~10,000)<br/>Dec 2023 – Jan 2025"]         CL["<b>Data cleaning and labels</b><br/>cropland only · irrigated / rainfed<br/>agricultural year → 8,781 parcels"]         SF["<b>Spatial folds</b><br/>20 km blocks → 5 balanced folds"]         TS["<b>Tile store</b> (Google Earth Engine)<br/>Sentinel-2 L2A + Cloud Score+ · Sentinel-1<br/>128 px tiles · 12 months × 19 bands"]         FE["<b>Parcel features</b><br/>monthly medians of S2 bands,<br/>indices and S1 backscatter"]         CH["<b>Chips p8 / p16</b><br/>64 × 64 px around each parcel,<br/>aligned to the model patches"]         GT --> CL --> SF --> TS         TS --> FE         TS --> CH     end      subgraph P2["Phase 2 · Model evaluation"]         BL["<b>S1/S2 baseline</b><br/>204 features per parcel"]         FM["<b>Foundation models (frozen)</b><br/>Clay · Prithvi-EO-2.0 · TerraMind · AgriFM<br/>→ one embedding per parcel"]         CF["<b>Classifiers</b><br/>LogReg · RF · HGB · SVM<br/>3 train / 1 validation / 1 test folds"]         CM["<b>Comparison</b><br/>same parcels · paired differences<br/>block-bootstrap 95% CI"]         BL --> CF         FM --> CF         CF --> CM     end      FE --> BL     CH --> FM     SF -. "folds" .-> CF     CM --> R(["Does a foundation model beat<br/>the Sentinel-1/2 baseline?"])

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
1. Labels. The Moroccan field survey (Ouassanouan et al., 2026) records crop type and irrigation system for each parcel. Cropland parcels are labelled irrigated (flood, sprinkler, drip, pivot and related systems) or rainfed. Rainfed parcels constitute 14% of the sample; macro-averaged metrics are therefore used so that both classes carry equal weight.

2. Spatial folds. Spatial autocorrelation between neighbouring parcels inflates accuracy when training and test parcels are adjacent (Roberts et al., 2017). The study area is therefore partitioned into 20 km blocks, and whole blocks are assigned to five folds. Every model is evaluated on blocks that were not used in training.

3. Common image store. For the agricultural year of each parcel (September–August), Sentinel-2 observations (cloud-masked with Cloud Score+) and Sentinel-1 backscatter are aggregated into 12 monthly composites and stored as non-overlapping 1.28 km tiles. The baseline and all foundation models read the same pixels, so that differences in performance are attributable to the representation rather than to the input data.

4. Parcel representations.

  • Feature baseline: for each of the 12 months, the median of the parcel's inner pixels for the Sentinel-2 bands, three spectral indices and Sentinel-1 backscatter, yielding 204 features. Months without clear observations are temporally interpolated.
  • Foundation-model embedding: a 64 × 64 px window (640 m) around the parcel is passed through the frozen encoder. The resulting patch embeddings are averaged with weights equal to the fraction of each patch inside the parcel. Clay, Prithvi-EO-2.0 and TerraMind are applied month by month; AgriFM processes the full year in one pass (Foundation models).

5. Temporal aggregation. A foundation model yields up to 12 × 1,024 values per parcel. Two aggregation schemes are evaluated:

  • PCA pipeline: monthly embeddings are concatenated and reduced to 128 principal components, fitted on the training folds only.
  • L-TAE pipeline (planned): a lightweight temporal attention encoder learns the relative importance of the months, following the PANGAEA benchmark protocol.

6. Classifiers. Four classifiers (logistic regression, random forest, histogram gradient boosting and a support vector machine) are trained on every representation with identical hyperparameter grids. Logistic regression on frozen embeddings corresponds to the standard linear probe and measures the information already present in the pretrained representation.

7. Evaluation. Five rotations are performed: three folds for training, one for hyperparameter selection and one for testing. Each parcel thus receives exactly one out-of-fold prediction from a model that was not trained on its block.

8. Comparison. All inputs are evaluated on the same parcels. Uncertainty is estimated with a block bootstrap (1,000 resamples of 20 km blocks), using identical resamples for every input so that differences are paired. A foundation model is considered superior only if the 95% confidence interval of the difference in macro-F1 excludes zero after Holm correction for multiple comparisons.

docs.title: Scope of inference
docs.text:
• The results quantify performance on unseen areas within the surveyed Moroccan regions.
  • They do not yet establish performance in other years or in other countries; these are addressed by RQ3 and RQ4.
  • Region and survey year are partly confounded (El Gharb and Tadla surveyed only in 2023/24, Souss only in 2024/25); differences between regions may therefore partly reflect differences between years.

docs.title: Heads and mapping: what GeoFM crop studies use
docs.text:
Literature search of 6 Nov 2026: which head is put on a GeoFM for crop classification, which neural baselines are used, and what wall-to-wall mapping requires. Result: decision D11.

Head Used for Papers Classical ML on frozen embeddings (LogReg, RF, GBDT, SVM, kNN) per-pixel / per-parcel classification Presto (Tseng et al. 2023); AlphaEarth irrigated vs rainfed (Yang et al. 2026); AlphaEarth cropland maps (Mughees et al. 2026); Galileo / CropFM + RF (Nedungadi et al. 2026) Small neural head (linear, MLP) per-pixel classification, fine-tuning TESSERA, 2-layer MLP per pixel (Feng et al. 2025); Presto / AlphaEarth + RF or MLP (Tong & Wang 2025); WorldCereal, fine-tuned Presto (Butsko et al. 2025) Segmentation decoder (UPerNet, UNet) wall-to-wall maps from patch-based models PANGAEA (Marsocci et al. 2024); Prithvi-EO-2.0 (Szwarcman et al. 2024) Neural baseline (from scratch) Input Gives maps Note TempCNN (Pelletier et al. 2019) pixel time series yes, per pixel 1D-CNN > RF for irrigated mapping (Bazzi et al. 2019); TempCNN-type models transfer better across regions than GeoFM embeddings (Tong & Wang 2025) L-TAE (Garnot & Landrieu 2020) pixel or parcel time series yes same module as the E03 pipeline U-TAE (Garnot & Landrieu 2021) image tiles yes, 10 m PASTIS baseline; counterpart of GeoFM + UPerNet PSE-TAE (Garnot et al. 2020) parcel pixel sets no (needs polygons) parcel-level only LSTM, Transformer (BreizhCrops, Rußwurm et al. 2020) pixel time series yes similar to TempCNN in benchmarks

Main points - Several 2025–26 studies find the head choice matters little on frozen embeddings (LogReg within 0.3 pp of a boosted ensemble, Mughees et al. 2026), but E01 shows RF is weaker on dense PCA embeddings, so the linear probe is the fairer headline for GeoFMs. - GeoFM embeddings degrade under large geographic shifts (cross-continent) more than simple temporal CNNs (Tong & Wang 2025): relevant for RQ4. - Fine-tuning helps in operational crop mapping (WorldCereal) but can collapse pretrained features without care (Nedungadi et al. 2026): relevant for RQ2.

docs.title: IrrMap · Mandal et al. (2025)
docs.text:
Citation

Mandal et al. (2025). IrrMap: a large-scale comprehensive dataset for irrigation method mapping. KDD 2025. arXiv:2505.08273 · data: Hugging Face

In one line: a large US dataset of image patches labelled with the irrigation method (flood, sprinkler, drip), built from state agricultural databases.

docs.title: What they did
docs.text:
• Labels from state datasets: Arizona (verified irrigated lands), Utah (Water-Related Land Use), Washington (WSDA agricultural land use), Colorado (CDSS).
  • Imagery: single Sentinel-2 scenes (cloud cover ≤ 5%) and Landsat, 11 Sentinel-2 bands, reprojected to EPSG:4326 and cut into 224 × 224 px patches on a fixed grid.
  • Classes: 0 none, 1 flood, 2 sprinkler, 3 drip; plus crop group and a cloud mask. No rainfed class.
  • Split: random 80 / 20 per state and year; U-Net models.

docs.title: Our check of their code and splits (Nov 2026)
docs.text:
• Every acquisition date is a separate sample, so the same place appears many times. Almost every test patch location also appears in training on another date (Washington 2018: 31,056 of 31,064; all states: 423,226 of 423,268). The test set is also used for evaluation after every epoch. Their scores are therefore not spatially independent.
  • Minor code issues (missing argparse import, undefined src_path, a constant land-type band).

docs.title: What this research takes from it
docs.text:
• Not usable as our dataset (no rainfed class), but its label sources are: eastern Washington (WSDA) and Utah (WRLU) contain both irrigated and dryland fields — candidate transfer regions (data sources, decision D10).
  • A concrete example of why spatial folds are needed (protocol §2).

docs.title: L-TAE · Garnot & Landrieu (2020)
docs.text:
Citation

Garnot, V. S. F., & Landrieu, L. (2020). Lightweight temporal self-attention for classifying satellite images time series. AALTD workshop, ECML-PKDD 2020. arXiv:2007.00586

In one line: a small temporal-attention module that learns which dates of a time series matter, and collapses the series into one vector.

docs.title: What they did
docs.text:
• Starts from the temporal attention encoder (TAE) of PSE-TAE and makes it lighter: each attention head has a single learnt master query instead of a query computed from the sequence; channels are split between heads.
  • A positional encoding of the acquisition date keeps the order of the observations.
  • Evaluated on parcel-level crop-type classification from Sentinel-2 time series.

docs.title: Key results
docs.text: • Matches or beats the heavier attention and recurrent models with far fewer parameters and less compute.

docs.title: What this research takes from it
docs.text:
• The temporal model of the L-TAE pipeline: attention over the 12 monthly embeddings of Clay, Prithvi and TerraMind, and over the 12 months of the S1/S2 features, so the baseline gets the same temporal model (E03, protocol §5).
  • Default size from the paper (16 heads, d_k 8, d_model 256, MLP 256–128).
  • PANGAEA uses the same module to aggregate dates for single-date GeoFMs (PANGAEA).

docs.title: Differences and limitations
docs.text: • Designed for raw reflectance time series of many dates; here it runs on 12 monthly composites or embeddings.

docs.title: Moroccan crop and irrigation survey · Ouassanouan et al. (2026)
docs.text:
Citation

Ouassanouan, Y., Elfarkh, J., Grich, S., Liblab, A., & Chehbouni, A. (2026). Crop and irrigation types ground-truth dataset for Moroccan agricultural regions. Scientific Data, 13, 746. doi:10.1038/s41597-026-06993-y · data: figshare, doi:10.6084/m9.figshare.28486022.v2

In one line: the first openly available, systematically collected parcel-level ground-truth dataset of crop types and irrigation systems for North Africa, and the source of all labels in this research.

docs.title: What they did
docs.text:
• Regions: five major agricultural regions of Morocco with contrasting climates and water sources: El Gharb (humid to sub-humid; rice, vegetables; surface water), Tadla (semi-arid to sub-humid; large-scale irrigation; sugar beet, cereals), Doukkala (Mediterranean, ~400 mm; mixed irrigated and rainfed systems), El Haouz (semi-arid, ~250 mm; olives, citrus; groundwater) and Souss (arid; drip-irrigated export crops).
  • Period: December 2023 – January 2025, i.e. two agricultural seasons.
  • Protocol: a standardised survey form built in QGIS and deployed offline in the QField mobile application, with Sentinel-2 false-colour composites (B11, B8, B2) as background. A team of four (the same persons throughout) digitised each parcel on site; two collectors recorded the parcels on either side of the route.
  • Attributes per parcel: polygon, crop type (45 types), agricultural class (seasonal crops, trees, trees + seasonal crops, weeds, bare soil, water bodies), irrigation system, geotagged photograph; for trees also height, crown diameter and row and tree spacing; contextual notes from farmer interviews where possible.
  • Irrigation systems: rainfed and six irrigated systems: flood (traditional surface), basin (structured flood), drip, sprinkler and centre pivot.

docs.title: Data records
docs.text: Record Content Shapefile about 10,000 parcel polygons with crop type, class and irrigation system Photographs one geotagged photo per parcel Sentinel-2 table mean Sentinel-2 bands (B2–B12) and NDVI per parcel for 2024

docs.title: Quality control
docs.text:
• Daily review of the collected data by the team; debriefing after each mission.
  • Post-processing: automated filtering and manual cleaning, removal of overlaps between polygons of different collectors, harmonisation of misspelled and overlapping class labels (e.g. "fruit trees" and "apple trees" merged into Trees), correction of clearly mislabelled parcels.
  • Consistency check with 2024 NDVI time series per class: bare soil 0.1–0.3 all year; seasonal crops 0.7–0.9 in the growing season and 0.1–0.3 from June to October; trees 0.7–0.8, falling to 0.5–0.6 in summer; weeds 0.2–0.4 in February–April.

docs.title: What this research takes from it
docs.text:
• Labels: the irrigation-system attribute defines the binary target. Any irrigated system = irrigated, rainfed = rainfed; only the cropland classes (seasonal crops, trees, trees + seasonal) are kept. After cleaning, 8,781 parcels remain (7,585 irrigated, 1,196 rainfed) (ML-ready dataset §4).
  • Agricultural year: the survey date assigns each parcel to the 2023/24 or 2024/25 season, and the imagery is taken from that season (D2).
  • Spatial validation: parcels were recorded along survey routes, so neighbouring parcels are clustered and usually share a class, which motivates the 20 km block cross-validation (dataset §5).
  • Imagery: the provided 2024 Sentinel-2 averages are not used; monthly composites are computed for each parcel's own agricultural year from Earth Engine (dataset §6).

docs.title: Differences and limitations
docs.text:
• Class imbalance and regional concentration: rainfed parcels form 14% of the cleaned cropland sample, and 1,122 of the 1,196 rainfed parcels lie in Doukkala; rainfed accuracy therefore largely reflects one region.
  • Region and season are confounded: El Gharb and Tadla were surveyed only in 2023/24 and Souss only in 2024/25.
  • Route-based sampling: parcels close to the survey routes are over-represented; the sample is not a probability sample of Moroccan cropland, so it cannot be used directly for unbiased area estimation (Phase 5).
  • Single-season labels: irrigation status is observed once and may change between years with water availability.
  • Validation of the labels is qualitative (photographs, NDVI consistency); no independent accuracy figure for the labels is reported. Remaining polygon overlaps were found in this research (six parcels fully covered by others; dataset §6.4).

docs.title: PANGAEA · Marsocci et al. (2024)
docs.text:
Citation

Marsocci, V., et al. (2024). PANGAEA: a global and inclusive benchmark for geospatial foundation models. arXiv. arXiv:2412.04204

In one line: a common benchmark that evaluates many geospatial foundation models in the same way, and finds that they do not consistently beat supervised models trained from scratch.

docs.title: What they did
docs.text:
• Many GeoFMs on a range of Earth-observation tasks (segmentation, change detection, regression), including the crop datasets PASTIS and a South Sudan crop-type set.
  • Frozen encoders with the same trainable decoder for every model (UPerNet).
  • Time series with single-date models: each date is encoded separately, then the dates are combined by a linear mapping or an L-TAE (L-TAE).
  • Supervised baselines trained from scratch (UNet, ViT); label-fraction experiments.

docs.title: Key results
docs.text:
• GeoFMs do not consistently outperform the supervised baselines.
  • They help most when labels are few.
  • L-TAE aggregation generally beats the linear mapping for multi-temporal tasks.
  • Adding SAR to optical input did not always help.

docs.title: What this research takes from it
docs.text:
• Frozen-encoder evaluation with an identical head for every model as the main comparison (protocol).
  • The L-TAE pipeline next to the PCA pipeline (E03, decision D8).
  • A result where GeoFMs only equal a strong baseline is a plausible outcome, not a failure (E01).
  • For maps: a segmentation head (UPerNet) on the frozen encoder (decision D11).

docs.title: Differences and limitations
docs.text: • Pixel-level segmentation benchmarks; this research classifies parcels (one label per field), so the "head" is a classifier on a pooled parcel embedding.

docs.title: PASTIS and U-TAE · Garnot & Landrieu (2021)
docs.text:
Citation

Garnot, V. S. F., & Landrieu, L. (2021). Panoptic segmentation of satellite image time series with convolutional temporal attention networks. ICCV 2021. arXiv:2107.07933

In one line: the reference benchmark for crop mapping from Sentinel-2 time series, with a spatio-temporal model (U-TAE) that segments whole image tiles.

docs.title: What they did
docs.text:
• PASTIS dataset: Sentinel-2 time series of agricultural parcels in France on 128 × 128 px patches, with crop-type labels per pixel and per parcel; the patches are split into 5 folds.
  • Fold rotation: in each round 3 folds train, 1 fold validates, 1 fold tests; all five rotations are reported.
  • U-TAE: a U-Net whose temporal dimension is collapsed by temporal self-attention (L-TAE) at the lowest resolution; the attention masks are reused at higher resolutions. Semantic and panoptic segmentation.

docs.title: Key results
docs.text: • U-TAE set the state of the art for semantic segmentation of crop types on PASTIS; the panoptic head separates individual parcels.

docs.title: What this research takes from it
docs.text:
• The PASTIS rotation (3 train / 1 validation / 1 test) for every model (decision D3, protocol §2).
  • Non-overlapping 128 px tiles as the shared image store (dataset pipeline).
  • U-TAE as a neural baseline for wall-to-wall maps (decision D11).

docs.title: Differences and limitations
docs.text: • Dense labels in France, many crop classes; this research has sparse parcel labels and two classes (irrigated, rainfed). Our folds are 20 km spatial blocks.

docs.title: Invariant features for crop classification · Tong & Wang (2025)
docs.text:
Citation

Tong, X.-Y., & Wang, S. (2025). Invariant features for global crop type classification. arXiv. arXiv:2509.03497

In one line: GeoFM embeddings work for transfer between nearby countries but break down across continents, where a simple temporal CNN on Sentinel-2 time series transfers better.

docs.title: What they did
docs.text:
• Crop-type classification with transfer across countries, continents and hemispheres.
  • Inputs and heads: Presto (128-d) and AlphaEarth (64-d) per-pixel embeddings with a random forest (500 trees) or an 8-layer MLP; harmonic features with RF / MLP; deep models on 5-day median Sentinel-2 series (CropNet with 2D spectral-temporal convolutions, a 1D variant, TempCNN, ResNet-50, EfficientNetV2-S, ConvNeXt-Tiny).
  • Time-series augmentation (time shift, time scale, magnitude warping).

docs.title: Key results
docs.text:
• GeoFM embeddings are competitive when the shift is mild (between countries).
  • They degrade strongly across continents and hemispheres (e.g. USA → Australia: overall accuracy 45% for Presto and 46% for AlphaEarth, against 87% for CropNet).
  • Simple 5-day Sentinel-2 series with CropNet beat harmonic features and GeoFM embeddings in every transfer setting; augmentation adds further gains. The authors conclude that inductive bias matters more than model scale or pretraining.

docs.title: What this research takes from it
docs.text:
• A temporal CNN (TempCNN) as neural baseline next to the GeoFMs (decision D11).
  • An expectation for RQ4: transfer to a region with different practices may favour simpler temporal models.

docs.title: Differences and limitations
docs.text: • Crop types, not irrigation; pixel-level; different label sources per country.

docs.title: AlphaEarth for irrigated mapping · Yang et al. (2026)
docs.text:
Citation

Yang, L., Gao, Y., Zhao, X., Liang, N., Ma, R., Xi, S., Zhang, X., & Wang, R. (2026). Evaluating the performance of AlphaEarth Foundation embeddings for irrigated cropland mapping across regions and years. Remote Sensing, 18(7), 1065. doi:10.3390/rs18071065

In one line: the closest study to this research — foundation-model embeddings for irrigated vs non-irrigated cropland, compared with Sentinel features and tested across years and regions.

docs.title: What they did
docs.text:
• Regions: Guanzhong Plain, China (main) and Kansas, USA (independent site); years 2022 and 2024, cross-year test on 2023.
  • Inputs: AlphaEarth embeddings vs Sentinel-1/2 features.
  • Classifiers on the embeddings: K-means, decision tree, random forest, gradient boosting (GBDT), linear SVM, RBF SVM, MLP.
  • Feature separability by Jeffries–Matusita distance.

docs.title: Key results
docs.text:
• Embeddings separate the classes better than Sentinel features (best embedding dimension JM 1.58 vs NDWI 0.72).
  • Overall accuracy about 0.95 in the Guanzhong Plain and 0.93 in Kansas; under GBDT, embeddings 0.95 vs Sentinel features 0.84. The paper's abstract, text and tables name different best classifiers (RF, GBDT, DT / RBF-SVM), so the "best head" is not clear-cut.
  • Unsupervised K-means already reaches 0.85 / 0.81.
  • Across years (train 2022, apply 2023 and 2024): stable, OA 0.87–0.88.
  • Across regions (train China, apply Kansas, no retraining): collapses to OA about 0.2–0.47, mostly missed irrigated fields — attributed to different irrigation regimes, phenology and management.

docs.title: What this research takes from it
docs.text:
• Several classifier heads on frozen embeddings, as in our parcel benchmark (E01).
  • A warning for RQ4: temporal transfer can be stable while spatial transfer fails; the transfer region must be close in irrigation practice (decision D10).

docs.title: Differences and limitations
docs.text:
• Two temperate regions and two to three years only; the contribution of each AlphaEarth input source cannot be separated.
  • Pixel-level task; this research classifies parcels and compares four open GeoFMs against a Sentinel baseline.

docs.title: Week 2026-W45 · first RQ1 result
docs.text: In one line: the frozen foundation models reach the accuracy of the Sentinel-1/2 baseline but do not beat it on average (macro-F1 ≈ 0.91); in the hardest region Clay and Prithvi hold up better than the baseline.

docs.title: 1. Done this week
docs.text:
• First complete RQ1 experiment on the final dataset (shared 128 px tile store, patch-aligned chips, 8,775 parcels, 5 spatial folds): baseline + 4 GeoFMs × 4 classifiers → E01 report.
  • Validation design fixed: PASTIS rotation (3 folds train, next fold validation, 1 fold test) for every model, classical and neural → decision D3. E01 used the earlier nested design; E02 repeats it with the final design.
  • Reproducible experiments: every run now comes from a config file in experiments/ and writes its report; any result can be rerun with one command.
  • Documentation: introduction, overview, evaluation protocol, decisions, results.
  • Literature: PANGAEA (how GeoFM benchmarks handle time series), PASTIS (fold rotation), IrrMap (US irrigation data) → literature notes.
  • Transfer data check (US): of the downloaded state datasets, eastern Washington (WSDA) and Utah (WRLU) contain both irrigated and dryland fields; the USGS and Colorado data are irrigated-only → decision D10.

docs.text:

Macro-F1, out-of-fold, same 8,775 parcels.

  • No GeoFM is significantly better than the baseline with any classifier. Clay + SVM (0.910) and the baseline
  • SVM (0.906) are level.
  • Linear probe: TerraMind and Clay equal the baseline, so the frozen embeddings already hold the irrigated / rainfed signal.

  • Hardest region (fold 0, rainfed fields in Doukkala and Souss): baseline 0.80; Prithvi 0.87 and Clay 0.86 (SVM).

docs.title: 3. To discuss / decide
docs.text:
1. Headline classifier. Keep RF (as in the proposal) plus the linear probe as headline, and report HGB / SVM as robustness checks? SVM is the best classifier for every input.
  2. Temporal aggregation. Add the L-TAE pipeline (E03, as in PANGAEA) next to the PCA pipeline, before starting LoRA fine-tuning?
  3. Transfer region (RQ4). Tunisia has 10 rainfed validation points; eastern Washington / Utah would give thousands and several years. Decide after RQ1–RQ2?
